bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Parity Rules in Sums
bradley_insight.content: Remember the basic arithmetic parity rules when finding the distribution of sums: $\text{Even} + \text{Even} = \text{Even}$ and $\text{Odd} + \text{Odd} = \text{Even}$, while $\text{Even} + \text{Odd} = \text{Odd}$. For conditional probability with discrete sums like $\text{P}(S \le 3 \mid S \text{ is even})$, always list the allowed sample space: since the minimum sum of two positive integers is $1 + 1 = 2$, the only even sum $\le 3$ is $S = 2$.

question:
The discrete random variable $T$ takes values $0, 1, 2, 3,$ and $4$ with probability distribution given by:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(T = t) &= k \times 2^t \cr &\quad \text{for } t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 \end{aligned}where $k$ is a constant.

(a) Show that $k = \dfrac{1}{31}$.

(b) Find $\text{P}(T \ge 2)$.

Two independent observations of $T$, denoted by $T_1$ and $T_2$, are recorded.

(c) Find the probability that the product $T_1 T_2 = 0$.

(d) Find the probability that $T_1 + T_2 = 4$, given that the product $T_1 T_2 > 0$.
steps:
(a) Showing $k = \dfrac{1}{31}$:

The probabilities must sum to $1$:\begin{aligned} &\sum_{t=0}^4 \text{P}(T = t) = 1 \cr &k(2^0 + 2^1 + 2^2 + 2^3 + 2^4) = 1 \cr &k(1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16) = 1 \cr &31k = 1 \cr &k = \dfrac{1}{31} \end{aligned}

(b) Finding $\text{P}(T \ge 2)$:

Using the complement rule:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(T \ge 2) \cr & \quad = 1 - [\text{P}(T = 0) + \text{P}(T = 1)] \cr & \quad = 1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{31} + \dfrac{2}{31}\right) \cr & \quad = 1 - \dfrac{3}{31} \cr & \quad = \dfrac{28}{31} \end{aligned}

(c) Finding $\text{P}(T_1 T_2 = 0)$:

The product is $0$ if at least one observation is $0$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(T = 0) &= \dfrac{1}{31} \cr \text{P}(T > 0) &= \dfrac{30}{31} \end{aligned}Using the complement rule:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(T_1 T_2 = 0) &= 1 - [\text{P}(T > 0)]^2 \cr &= 1 - \left(\dfrac{30}{31}\right)^2 \cr &= 1 - \dfrac{900}{961} \cr &= \dfrac{61}{961} \end{aligned}

(d) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(T_1 + T_2 = 4 \mid T_1 T_2 > 0)$:

The condition $T_1 T_2 > 0$ restricts both observations to $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(T_1 T_2 > 0) &= \left(\dfrac{30}{31}\right)^2 \cr &= \dfrac{900}{961} \end{aligned}The non-zero pairs summing to $4$ are $(1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1)$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(1, 3) = \dfrac{2}{31} \times \dfrac{8}{31} = \dfrac{16}{961} \cr &\text{P}(2, 2) = \left(\dfrac{4}{31}\right)^2 = \dfrac{16}{961} \cr &\text{P}(3, 1) = \dfrac{8}{31} \times \dfrac{2}{31} = \dfrac{16}{961} \end{aligned}Summing the pairs:\begin{aligned} \text{Numerator} &= \dfrac{16 + 16 + 16}{961} \cr &= \dfrac{48}{961} \end{aligned}Calculate the conditional quotient:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(T_1 + T_2 = 4 \mid T_1 T_2 > 0) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{48 / 961}{900 / 961} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{48}{900} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4}{75} \cr &\quad \approx 0.0533\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Show that completed, (b) 28/31, (c) 61/961, (d) 4/75

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), $1/961 = (1/31)^2$ only considers the single outcome $(0, 0)$. The product is also zero when one observation is 0 and the other is non-zero, giving $1 - (30/31)^2 = 61/961$.

In part (d), $48/961$ is the unconditional probability $\text{P}(T_1 + T_2 = 4 \cap T_1 T_2 > 0)$. You must divide by the conditioning probability $\text{P}(T_1 T_2 > 0) = 900/961$, simplifying to $48/900 = 4/75$.
In part (b), $3/31$ is $\text{P}(T \le 1)$. For $\text{P}(T \ge 2)$, subtract this from 1 to obtain $28/31$. In (d), forgetting the pair $(2, 2)$ omits $16/961$ from the numerator.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Product Greater Than Zero as a Condition
bradley_insight.content: When given that $T_1 T_2 > 0$, notice how this immediately simplifies the problem: it simply means that zero is excluded from both observations! The conditioning denominator is $[\text{P}(T > 0)]^2 = (30/31)^2$. When finding pairs that sum to $4$, you only need to check combinations of $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, which prevents you from accidentally including $(0, 4)$ or $(4, 0)$.

question:
A software testing team models the number of test cycles, $N$, until a critical software bug is triggered as a geometric distribution with probability mass function:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(N = n) &= (0.85)^{n-1}(0.15) \cr &\quad \text{for } n = 1, 2, 3, \dots \end{aligned}(a) By considering an infinite geometric series, show that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \text{P}(N = n) = 1$.

(b) Find the probability that the bug is triggered within the first $4$ test cycles ($ ext{P}(N \le 4)$).

(c) Show that for any positive integers $k$ and $m$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(N > k + m \mid N > k) \cr &\quad = \text{P}(N > m) \end{aligned}and evaluate this probability when $k = 5$ and $m = 3$.

(d) State the name of this probability property, and explain why this model may be inappropriate for physical machinery subject to mechanical wear and tear.
steps:
(a) Showing the Probabilities Sum to 1:

The probabilities form an infinite geometric series with $a = 0.15$ and $r = 0.85$:\begin{aligned} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \text{P}(N = n) &= \sum_{n=1}^\infty 0.15(0.85)^{n-1} \cr &= \dfrac{a}{1 - r} \cr &= \dfrac{0.15}{1 - 0.85} \cr &= \dfrac{0.15}{0.15} \cr &= 1 \end{aligned}

(b) Finding $\text{P}(N \le 4)$:

The bug occurs on or before cycle $4$ if the first $4$ cycles are not all bug-free:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(N \le 4) &= 1 - \text{P}(N > 4) \cr &= 1 - (0.85)^4 \cr &= 1 - 0.522006 \cr &= 0.47799 \cr &\approx 0.478\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(c) Deriving the Memoryless Property:

For any positive integer $t$, $\text{P}(N > t) = (0.85)^t$.

Using the definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(N > k + m \mid N > k) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{P}(N > k + m)}{\text{P}(N > k)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{(0.85)^{k+m}}{(0.85)^k} \cr &\quad = (0.85)^m \cr &\quad = \text{P}(N > m) \end{aligned}Evaluating for $k = 5$ and $m = 3$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(N > 8 \mid N > 5) &= (0.85)^3 \cr &= 0.614125 \cr &\approx 0.614\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(d) Name of Property and Physical Limitation:

This is the memoryless property.

It is inappropriate for physical machinery because physical components suffer from mechanical wear, friction, and thermal fatigue over time.

In reality, the probability of failure increases as a component ages, rather than remaining constant independently of its past operating history.
Final Answer: (a) Show that completed, (b) 0.478, (c) 0.614, (d) Memoryless property; machinery wears out so failure probability increases with age

pi_options.ans: (a) Show that completed, (b) 0.522, (c) 0.614, (d) Memoryless property; machinery wears out so failure probability increases with age
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), $0.522$ is $\text{P}(N > 4) = 0.85^4$, the probability that the bug is *not* triggered in the first 4 cycles. For $\text{P}(N \le 4)$, subtract this from 1 to obtain $0.478$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Show that completed, (b) 0.478, (c) 0.272, (d) Central Limit Theorem; sample size is too small
pi_options.feedback: In part (c), evaluating $(0.85)^8 = 0.272$ calculates the unconditional probability $\text{P}(N > 8)$. The conditional probability simplifies by index laws to $(0.85)^3 = 0.614$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Show that completed, (b) 0.478, (c) 0.614, (d) Law of large numbers; software code does not degrade over time
pi_options.feedback: The mathematical property shown in part (c) is the memoryless property of the geometric distribution, not the law of large numbers.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Memoryless Property
bradley_insight.content: The geometric distribution is the ONLY discrete distribution that possesses the memoryless property: \begin{aligned}&\text{P}(N > k + m \mid N > k)  \cr & \qquad \quad = \text{P}(N > m)\end{aligned} This means the system 'forgets' that it has already survived $k$ steps. It is a fantastic model for random electronic glitches or coin tosses, but highly unrealistic for mechanical engines, car batteries, or light bulbs that experience physical wear and tear.

question:
Two players, Alice and Bob, each roll an independent four-sided die with faces numbered $1, 2, 3,$ and $4$.

Bob's die is fair, so each score has a probability of $0.25$.

Alice's die has the probability distribution shown in the table below:
$a$$\text{P}(A = a)$
$1$$0.1$
$2$$0.2$
$3$$0.3$
$4$$0.4$
Let $A$ be Alice's score and $B$ be Bob's score.

(a) Find the probability that Alice and Bob roll the same score ($\text{P}(A = B)$).

(b) Find the probability that Alice's score is strictly greater than Bob's score ($\text{P}(A > B)$).

(c) Given that Alice's score is strictly greater than Bob's score, find the probability that the difference between their scores is at least $2$ ($\text{P}(A - B \ge 2 \mid A > B)$).
steps:
(a) Probability of Equal Scores $\text{P}(A = B)$:

Factoring out Bob's constant probability of $0.25$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A = B) &= 0.25(0.1 + 0.2 \cr & \quad + 0.3 + 0.4) \cr &= 0.25(1.0) \cr &= 0.25 \end{aligned}

(b) Probability that $A > B$:

Calculate the probabilities for each value of $A$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(A = 2, B = 1) \cr &\quad = 0.2(0.25) = 0.05 \cr &\text{P}(A = 3, B \le 2) \cr &\quad = 0.3(0.50) = 0.15 \cr &\text{P}(A = 4, B \le 3) \cr &\quad = 0.4(0.75) = 0.30 \end{aligned}Summing the probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A > B) &= 0.05 + 0.15 + 0.30 \cr &= 0.50 \end{aligned}

(c) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(A - B \ge 2 \mid A > B)$:

The pairs where $A - B \ge 2$ and $A > B$ are $(3, 1), (4, 1), (4, 2)$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(A = 3, B = 1):\cr 0.3(0.25) & \qquad= 0.075 \cr &\text{P}(A = 4, B = 1):\cr 0.4(0.25)& \qquad = 0.100 \cr &\text{P}(A = 4, B = 2):\cr 0.4(0.25) & \qquad= 0.100 \end{aligned}Summing the pairs:\begin{aligned} &\text{Numerator}\cr &= 0.075 + 0.100 + 0.100 = 0.275 \end{aligned}Using $\text{P}(A > B) = 0.50$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A - B \ge 2 \mid A > B) &= \dfrac{0.275}{0.50} \cr &= 0.55 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) 0.25, (b) 0.50, (c) 0.55

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), $0.275$ is the unconditional probability $\text{P}(A - B \ge 2)$. You must divide by the conditioning probability $\text{P}(A > B) = 0.50$, yielding $0.275 / 0.50 = 0.55$.
In part (b), $0.375$ would be the result if both dice were fair ($6/16$). Because Alice's die is biased towards higher numbers ($3$ and $4$), her probability of beating Bob is $0.50$.

In part (a), factoring out $0.25$ reveals that \begin{aligned}\text{P}(A = B) & = 0.25 \sum \text{P}(A = k) \cr & = 0.25(1)\cr & = 0.25\end{aligned} not $0.10$. In (c), forgetting the pair $(3, 1)$ underestimates the conditional probability.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Factoring Uniform Variables
bradley_insight.content: When one random variable is discrete uniform (like Bob's fair die with $\text{P}(B = b) = 0.25$), notice the elegant algebraic simplification in part (a): \begin{aligned}\sum \text{P}(A = k)\text{P}(B = k)& \qquad = 0.25 \sum \text{P}(A = k)& \qquad= 0.25(1) & \qquad= 0.25\end{aligned} No matter how wildly Alice's die is biased, the probability of rolling the same score against a fair $4$-sided die is ALWAYS $\frac{1}{4}$!

question:
A fairground attraction features a prize wheel that awards a prize multiplier $M \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$ with probabilities defined by the recurrence relation:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(M = 2m) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\text{P}(M = m) \cr &\quad \text{for } m \in \{1, 2, 4\} \end{aligned}Let $\text{P}(M = 1) = k$.

(a) Show that $k = \dfrac{8}{15}$, and write down the complete probability distribution of $M$.

(b) Calculate the expected value, $\text{E}(M)$.

(c) Calculate the variance, $\text{Var}(M)$.

(d) It costs $£2.50$ to play the game once, and the prize awarded is $£1.00 \times M$.
(i) Determine the expected financial loss per game for a player.
(ii) State the stake price that the fairground operator should charge to make the game mathematically fair.
steps:
(a) Showing $k = \dfrac{8}{15}$ and Distribution:

Express each outcome in terms of $k$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(M = 1) = k \cr &\text{P}(M = 2) = \dfrac{k}{2} \cr &\text{P}(M = 4) = \dfrac{k}{4} \cr &\text{P}(M = 8) = \dfrac{k}{8} \end{aligned}Summing the terms:\begin{aligned} k\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8}\right) &= 1 \cr k\left(\dfrac{15}{8}\right) &= 1 \cr k &= \dfrac{8}{15} \end{aligned}The complete probability distribution is:
$m$$\text{P}(M = m)$
$1$$\dfrac{8}{15}$
$2$$\dfrac{4}{15}$
$4$$\dfrac{2}{15}$
$8$$\dfrac{1}{15}$

(b) Expected Value $\text{E}(M)$:

\begin{aligned} \text{E}(M) &= \sum m\,\text{P}(M = m) \cr &= 1\left(\dfrac{8}{15}\right) + 2\left(\dfrac{4}{15}\right) \cr &\quad + 4\left(\dfrac{2}{15}\right) + 8\left(\dfrac{1}{15}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{8 + 8 + 8 + 8}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{32}{15} \cr &\approx 2.133 \end{aligned}

(c) Variance $\text{Var}(M)$:

First calculate $\text{E}(M^2)$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(M^2) &= \sum m^2\,\text{P}(M = m) \cr &= 1(8/15) + 4(4/15) \cr &\quad + 16(2/15) + 64(1/15) \cr &= \dfrac{8 + 16 + 32 + 64}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{120}{15} \cr &= 8 \end{aligned}Now compute $\text{Var}(M)$:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(M) &= 8 - \left(\dfrac{32}{15}\right)^2 \cr &= 8 - \dfrac{1024}{225} \cr &= \dfrac{1800 - 1024}{225} \cr &= \dfrac{776}{225} \cr &\approx 3.449\text{ (or } 3.45\text{)} \end{aligned}

(d)(i) Expected Financial Loss:

The expected payout is $£1.00 \times \frac{32}{15} \approx £2.1333$.\begin{aligned} \text{Expected Loss} &= £2.50 - £2.1333 \cr &= £0.3667 \cr &\approx £0.37 \end{aligned}

(d)(ii) Stake for a Mathematically Fair Game:

A fair game requires expected profit to be zero, so the stake equals the expected payout:\begin{aligned} \text{Fair Stake} &= £\dfrac{32}{15} \cr &\approx £2.13 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), $8$ is $\text{E}(M^2)$. You must subtract $[\text{E}(M)]^2 = (32/15)^2 = 1024/225$ to obtain $\text{Var}(M) = 776/225 \approx 3.45$.
In part (d), rounding the expected payout down to £2.00 is incorrect. The expected payout is $£32/15 \approx £2.133$, leaving an expected loss of $£2.50 - £2.133 = £0.37$ and a fair stake of $£2.13$.

In part (a), the recurrence relation states that $\text{P}(M = 2m) = \frac{1}{2}\text{P}(M = m)$, meaning probabilities *halve* as the multiplier doubles. Setting $\text{P}(M = 1) = 1/15$ reverses the powers.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: What 'Fair Game' Actually Means
bradley_insight.content: In probability and financial mathematics, a 'fair game' does NOT mean equal probability of winning and losing. It means that the expected financial return is zero: $\text{E}(\text{Profit}) = 0$, which requires that $\text{Stake} = \text{Expected Payout}$. If a game pays out an expected $£2.13$, charging a stake of $£2.13$ makes it mathematically fair.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The probability that an electronic component manufactured on a production line is defective is $0.2$, independently of other components.

(a) A large batch of $500$ components is inspected. The random variable $Y$ denotes the number of defective components in the batch.

Using a suitable Normal approximation, find the integer value of $a$ such that $\text{P}(Y \le a) \approx 0.95$.

In the expansion of $(0.2 + 0.8)^{60}$, the terms involving $0.2^r$ and $0.2^{r+1}$ are denoted by $T_r$ and $T_{r+1}$ respectively.

(b) Show that:
$$\dfrac{T_r}{T_{r+1}} = \dfrac{4(r + 1)}{60 - r}$$
(c) The number of defective components in a random sample of $60$ components is modelled by the random variable $X$.

(i) Find the set of integer values of $r$ for which $\text{P}(X = r) \le \text{P}(X = r + 1)$.

(ii) Hence determine the most likely number of defective components in the sample of $60$.
steps:
(a) Normal Approximation to the Binomial:

For $Y \sim \text{B}(500, 0.2)$, calculate the mean and variance:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 500(0.2) \cr &= 100 \cr \sigma^2 &= 100(0.8) \cr &= 80 \end{aligned}
Approximate $Y$ by $Y_{\text{norm}} \sim \text{N}(100, 80)$.

Applying a continuity correction gives $\text{P}(Y_{\text{norm}} \le a + 0.5) = 0.95$.

Standardising and solving for $a$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{a + 0.5 - 100}{\sqrt{80}} = 1.6449 \cr &a - 99.5 = 14.712 \cr &a = 114.212 \end{aligned}
Hence, to the nearest integer, $a = 114$.

(b) Successive Binomial Term Ratio:

The general terms are defined as:
$$T_r = \binom{60}{r}(0.2)^r (0.8)^{60-r}$$
$$T_{r+1} = \binom{60}{r+1}(0.2)^{r+1} (0.8)^{59-r}$$
Simplifying the combination ratio:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\binom{60}{r}}{\binom{60}{r+1}} &= \dfrac{(r+1)!}{r!} \times \dfrac{(59-r)!}{(60-r)!} \cr &= (r + 1) \times \dfrac{1}{60 - r} \cr &= \dfrac{r + 1}{60 - r} \end{aligned}
Simplifying the powers of probabilities:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{0.8^{60-r} (0.2)^r}{0.8^{59-r} (0.2)^{r+1}} &= \dfrac{0.8}{0.2} \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}
Multiplying the two results gives:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{T_r}{T_{r+1}} &= \left(\dfrac{r+1}{60-r}\right) \times 4 \cr &= \dfrac{4(r+1)}{60-r} \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Solving the Probability Inequality:

We require $\frac{T_r}{T_{r+1}} \le 1$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{4(r+1)}{60-r} \le 1 \cr &4r + 4 \le 60 - r \cr &5r \le 56 \cr &r \le 11.2 \end{aligned}
Since $r$ is an integer in $0 \le r \le 59$:
$$r \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots, 11\}$$

(c)(ii) Determining the Mode:

Probabilities increase for all integers up to $r = 11$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X = 11) \le \text{P}(X = 12) \end{aligned}
For $r \ge 12$, the ratio exceeds $1$, meaning:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X = 12) > \text{P}(X = 13) \end{aligned}
Probabilities decrease strictly thereafter.

Therefore, the most likely number of defective components is $12$.
Final Answer: (a) $a = 114$, (c)(i) $r \in \{0, 1, \dots, 11\}$, (ii) $12$

pi_options.feedback: Omission of the continuity correction $+0.5$ leads to $\frac{a - 100}{\sqrt{80}} = 1.6449$, giving $a \approx 114.71 \approx 115$.
Confusing the upper bound index where growth stops ($r = 11$) with the resulting peak outcome gives $11$ instead of $r + 1 = 12$.
Incorrectly rounding $11.2$ up to include $12$ in the increasing phase violates the inequality, since at $r = 12$ the ratio exceeds $1$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Off-By-One Mode Trap
bradley_insight.content: When solving $\text{P}(X = r) \le \text{P}(X = r + 1)$, remember what the final inequality means. If the inequality holds for $r \le 11$, setting $r = 11$ gives $\text{P}(X = 11) \le \text{P}(X = 12)$. The chain of probabilities climbs all the way up to $X = 12$. A common slip is writing down $11$ as the mode because $11$ was the largest integer in your solution set for $r$. Always write out the final step $\text{P}(11) \le \text{P}(12)$ to avoid losing the final accuracy mark.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The probability that an unsolicited telephone call made by a contact centre results in an appointment is $0.25$, independently of all other calls.

(a) An agent makes $480$ calls over the course of a month. The random variable $Y$ denotes the total number of appointments made.

Using a suitable Normal approximation with a continuity correction, calculate the probability that the agent makes at least $130$ appointments. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

(b) In a focused morning session, an agent makes a smaller sample of $39$ calls. The random variable $X$ denotes the number of appointments secured, so that $X \sim \text{B}(39, 0.25)$.

By considering the ratio of consecutive probabilities, show that:
$$\dfrac{\text{P}(X = r + 1)}{\text{P}(X = r)} = \dfrac{39 - r}{3(r + 1)}$$
(c)
(i) Determine the integer value of $r$ for which $\text{P}(X = r + 1) = \text{P}(X = r)$.

(ii) Hence identify all values of $X$ that are most likely to occur, and explain why this distribution is bimodal.
steps:
(a) Normal Approximation with Continuity Correction:

For $Y \sim \text{B}(480, 0.25)$, find parameters:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 480(0.25) \cr &= 120 \cr \sigma^2 &= 120(0.75) \cr &= 90 \end{aligned}
Approximate $Y$ by $Y_{\text{norm}} \sim \text{N}(120, 90)$.

Applying a continuity correction for $\text{P}(Y \ge 130)$ gives $\text{P}(Y_{\text{norm}} \ge 129.5)$.

Standardising:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{129.5 - 120}{\sqrt{90}} \cr &= \dfrac{9.5}{9.4868} \cr &\approx 1.0014 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the tail probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(Z \ge 1.0014) \cr &\quad = 1 - \Phi(1.0014) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.8417 \cr &\quad = 0.158 \end{aligned}

(b) Consecutive Probability Ratio Derivation:

For $X \sim \text{B}(39, 0.25)$, take the ratio of consecutive terms:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{P}(X = r + 1)}{\text{P}(X = r)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\binom{39}{r+1}}{\binom{39}{r}} \times \dfrac{0.25}{0.75} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{39 - r}{r + 1} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{39 - r}{3(r + 1)} \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Finding Equality of Consecutive Terms:

Set the consecutive ratio equal to $1$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{39 - r}{3(r + 1)} = 1 \cr &39 - r = 3r + 3 \cr &4r = 36 \cr &r = 9 \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Identification of the Two Modes:

At $r = 9$, the ratio equals $1$, which gives:
$$\text{P}(X = 10) = \text{P}(X = 9)$$
For $r < 9$, the ratio exceeds $1$, so $\text{P}(X = r + 1) > \text{P}(X = r)$.

For $r > 9$, the ratio is less than $1$, so $\text{P}(X = r + 1) < \text{P}(X = r)$.

Therefore, the maximum probability occurs equally at $X = 9$ and $X = 10$, making the distribution bimodal.
Final Answer: (a) $0.158$, (c)(i) $r = 9$, (ii) $9$ and $10$

pi_options.feedback: Using an incorrect continuity correction of $130.5$ instead of $129.5$ gives $z = 1.054$ and probability $0.146$.
Overlooking that the ratio equals $1$ at $r = 9$ neglects the exact equality $\text{P}(X = 9) = \text{P}(X = 10)$, missing the bimodal nature.
An algebraic error when expanding $3(r + 1)$ as $3r - 3$ incorrectly yields $4r = 42$ and an incorrect index.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Integer Products and Bimodality
bradley_insight.content: A Binomial distribution $\text{B}(n, p)$ is bimodal if and only if $(n + 1)p$ is an integer. When $(n + 1)p = k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$, the ratio $\frac{\text{P}(X = k)}{\text{P}(X = k - 1)} = 1$, which produces two equal modal peaks at $X = k - 1$ and $X = k$. Here, $(39 + 1)(0.25) = 10$, creating identical peaks at $X = 9$ and $X = 10$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A wildlife sanctuary monitors a colony of a rare bird species. The probability that an egg in a nest hatches successfully is $\dfrac{2}{3}$, independently of all other eggs.

(a) During a breeding season, the sanctuary monitors $270$ separate nests, each containing a single egg. The random variable $Y$ denotes the total number of successfully hatched eggs.

Using a suitable Normal approximation with a continuity correction, find the integer value of $k$ such that $\text{P}(Y < k) \approx 0.025$.

(b) For a smaller isolated group of $40$ nests, each containing a single egg, the random variable $X$ models the number of eggs that hatch successfully, so that $X \sim \text{B}\left(40, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$.

Show that:
$$\dfrac{\text{P}(X = r + 1)}{\text{P}(X = r)} = \dfrac{2(40 - r)}{r + 1}$$
(c)
(i) Find all integer values of $r$ for which $\text{P}(X = r + 1) \ge \text{P}(X = r)$.

(ii) Hence find the most likely number of eggs to hatch in this group of $40$ nests, and find the exact value of the ratio $\dfrac{\text{P}(X = \text{mode})}{\text{P}(X = \text{mode} - 1)}$ as an irreducible fraction.
steps:
(a) Normal Approximation Threshold:

For $Y \sim \text{B}\left(270, \frac{2}{3}\right)$, calculate parameters:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 270\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \cr &= 180 \cr \sigma^2 &= 180\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \cr &= 60 \end{aligned}
Note that $Y < k \iff Y \le k - 1$.

Applying a continuity correction gives $\text{P}(Y_{\text{norm}} \le k - 0.5) = 0.025$.

Standardising and solving for $k$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{k - 0.5 - 180}{\sqrt{60}} = -1.960 \cr &k - 180.5 = -15.182 \cr &k = 165.318 \end{aligned}
To the nearest integer, $k = 165$.

(b) Consecutive Probability Ratio:

For $X \sim \text{B}\left(40, \frac{2}{3}\right)$, take consecutive terms:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{P}(X = r + 1)}{\text{P}(X = r)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\binom{40}{r+1}}{\binom{40}{r}} \times \dfrac{2/3}{1/3} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{40 - r}{r + 1} \times 2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2(40 - r)}{r + 1} \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Solving the Probability Inequality:

Solve $\text{P}(X = r + 1) \ge \text{P}(X = r)$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{2(40 - r)}{r + 1} \ge 1 \cr &80 - 2r \ge r + 1 \cr &3r \le 79 \cr &r \le 26.33 \end{aligned}
For integer $r$, $r \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots, 26\}$.

(c)(ii) Finding the Mode and Probability Ratio:

Probabilities increase strictly up to $r = 26$, so $\text{P}(X = 26) < \text{P}(X = 27)$.

For $r \ge 27$, probabilities decrease, so the mode is $27$.

Evaluating the ratio at the modal peak:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{P}(X = 27)}{\text{P}(X = 26)} &= \dfrac{2(40 - 26)}{26 + 1} \cr &= \dfrac{2(14)}{27} \cr &= \dfrac{28}{27} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $k = 165$, (c)(i) $r \in \{0, 1, \dots, 26\}$, (ii) Mode $= 27$, ratio $= \dfrac{28}{27}$

pi_options.feedback: Using an incorrect continuity correction of $k + 0.5$ instead of $k - 0.5$ for $Y < k$ leads to $k = 164$.
Confusing the upper index of increase ($r = 26$) with the mode selects $26$ and inverts the required probability ratio.
Rounding $79/3 \approx 26.33$ up to $27$ erroneously includes $r = 27$ in the set where probabilities are still increasing.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Continuity Corrections on Strict Inequalities
bradley_insight.content: For a discrete variable $Y$, the strict inequality $Y < k$ translates to $Y \le k - 1$. The upper boundary of the discrete bar at $k - 1$ is $(k - 1) + 0.5 = k - 0.5$. Writing $k + 0.5$ is a standard mistake that treats the strict inequality as a non-strict inequality and shifts your critical threshold by an entire unit.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A clinical trial investigates the efficacy of a treatment for a specific condition. The probability that an administered patient experiences complete recovery without side effects is $p = 0.4$, independently of other patients.

(a) In an extensive multicentre trial involving $300$ patients, the number of patients who recover completely without side effects is denoted by $Y \sim \text{B}(300, 0.4)$.

Using a suitable Normal approximation, calculate an estimate for the probability that between $110$ and $135$ patients (inclusive) achieve complete recovery without side effects. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

(b) For a general binomial random variable $X \sim \text{B}(n, p)$, where $0 < p < 1$ and $q = 1 - p$:
Show from the definition of the binomial probability mass function that:\begin{aligned) &\dfrac{\text{P}(X = r + 1)}{\text{P}(X = r)} \cr & \qquad \quad = \left(\dfrac{n - r}{r + 1}\right)\left(\dfrac{p}{q}\right)\end{aligned}(c)
(i) Deduce that $\text{P}(X = r + 1) > \text{P}(X = r)$ if and only if $r < (n + 1)p - 1$.

(ii) A secondary trial is conducted with $n = 74$ patients and $p = 0.4$. Use the condition in part (c)(i) to determine the most likely number(s) of complete recoveries.
steps:
(a) Normal Approximation for an Interval:

For $Y \sim \text{B}(300, 0.4)$, calculate parameters:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 300(0.4) \cr &= 120 \cr \sigma^2 &= 120(0.6) \cr &= 72 \end{aligned}
Applying continuity corrections for $110 \le Y \le 135$ gives $\text{P}(109.5 \le Y_{\text{norm}} \le 135.5)$.

Standardising both endpoints:\begin{aligned} z_1 &= \dfrac{109.5 - 120}{\sqrt{72}} \cr &\approx -1.237 \cr z_2 &= \dfrac{135.5 - 120}{\sqrt{72}} \cr &\approx 1.827 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the interval probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(-1.237 \le Z \le 1.827) \cr &\quad = \Phi(1.827) - \Phi(-1.237) \cr &\quad = 0.9661 - 0.1080 \cr &\quad = 0.858 \end{aligned}

(b) General Successive Ratio Proof:

Evaluate the combination ratio and probability ratio separately:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\binom{n}{r+1}}{\binom{n}{r}} &= \dfrac{n - r}{r + 1} \cr \dfrac{p^{r+1} q^{n-r-1}}{p^r q^{n-r}} &= \dfrac{p}{q} \end{aligned}
Multiplying these components directly gives:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{P}(X = r + 1)}{\text{P}(X = r)} &= \left(\dfrac{n - r}{r + 1}\right)\left(\dfrac{p}{q}\right) \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Inequality Deduction:

Set the consecutive ratio strictly greater than $1$:\begin{aligned} &\left(\dfrac{n - r}{r + 1}\right)\left(\dfrac{p}{q}\right) > 1 \cr &(n - r)p > (r + 1)q \cr &np - rp > rq + q \cr &np - q > r(p + q) \cr &np - (1 - p) > r(1) \cr &r < (n + 1)p - 1 \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Determining the Mode(s):

For $n = 74$ and $p = 0.4$:\begin{aligned} (n + 1)p - 1 &= 75(0.4) - 1 \cr &= 30 - 1 \cr &= 29 \end{aligned}
For $r < 29$ (integers $r \le 28$), probabilities increase strictly up to $X = 29$.

At $r = 29$, the ratio equals $1$, which gives:
$$\text{P}(X = 30) = \text{P}(X = 29)$$
For $r \ge 30$, the ratio is strictly less than $1$, so probabilities decrease thereafter.

Therefore, the distribution is bimodal with joint modes at $29$ and $30$.
Final Answer: (a) $0.858$, (c)(ii) $29$ and $30$

pi_options.feedback: Assuming that $r < 29$ strictly isolates $X = 30$ overlooks that when $r = 29$ the ratio equals $1$, making $29$ and $30$ equal modes.
Neglecting the continuity corrections entirely and evaluating between $110$ and $135$ gives $z_1 = -1.179$ and $z_2 = 1.768$, yielding $0.835$.
Selecting $29$ alone fails to observe that $r = 29$ yields $\text{P}(X = 30) = \text{P}(X = 29)$, so $30$ is also a modal peak.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Deriving the Binomial Mode Rule
bradley_insight.content: The relation $r < (n + 1)p - 1$ is a powerful result. If $(n + 1)p$ is not an integer, the floor $\lfloor (n + 1)p \rfloor$ gives the unique mode. If $(n + 1)p$ is an integer $m$, the probabilities at $m - 1$ and $m$ are identical, creating two modes. Keeping $p + q = 1$ in mind when rearranging $(n - r)p > (r + 1)q$ avoids messy fraction algebra.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A manufacturing process produces high-precision ceramic tiles. The probability that any tile has a surface flaw is $0.08$, independently of all other tiles.

(a) In a production run of $800$ tiles, the random variable $Y$ denotes the number of flawed tiles.

Using a suitable Normal approximation with a continuity correction, calculate the probability that the number of flawed tiles lies strictly within $1$ standard deviation of the mean. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

(b) A quality control technician takes a smaller random sample of $50$ tiles. The random variable $X$ denotes the number of flawed tiles in this sample, so that $X \sim \text{B}(50, 0.08)$.

(i) Show that $\dfrac{\text{P}(X = r + 1)}{\text{P}(X = r)} = \dfrac{2(50 - r)}{23(r + 1)}$.

(ii) Prove that $\text{P}(X = r)$ is strictly decreasing for all integers $r \ge 4$.

(iii) Hence determine the mode of $X$, and calculate $\text{P}(X = \text{mode})$ correct to 4 decimal places.
steps:
(a) Normal Approximation within 1 Standard Deviation:

For $Y \sim \text{B}(800, 0.08)$, calculate parameters:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 800(0.08) \cr &= 64 \cr \sigma^2 &= 64(0.92) \cr &= 58.88 \cr \sigma &= \sqrt{58.88} \cr &\approx 7.673 \end{aligned}
The interval within $1$ standard deviation is:\begin{aligned} \mu - \sigma &= 64 - 7.673 \cr &= 56.327 \cr \mu + \sigma &= 64 + 7.673 \cr &= 71.673 \end{aligned}
The discrete integers in this range are $57 \le Y \le 71$.

Applying continuity corrections gives $\text{P}(56.5 \le Y_{\text{norm}} \le 71.5)$.

Standardising:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{71.5 - 64}{7.673} \cr &\approx 0.9775 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the symmetric tail probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(-0.9775 \le Z \le 0.9775) \cr &\quad = 2\Phi(0.9775) - 1 \cr &\quad = 2(0.8358) - 1 \cr &\quad = 0.672 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Consecutive Probability Ratio:

With $p = 0.08$ and $q = 0.92$, the parameter ratio is $\frac{p}{q} = \frac{0.08}{0.92} = \frac{2}{23}$.

Taking consecutive terms:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{P}(X = r + 1)}{\text{P}(X = r)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{50 - r}{r + 1} \times \dfrac{2}{23} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2(50 - r)}{23(r + 1)} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Proof of Strictly Decreasing Sequence for $r \ge 4$:

Probabilities strictly decrease when the ratio is less than $1$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{2(50 - r)}{23(r + 1)} < 1 \cr &100 - 2r < 23r + 23 \cr &25r > 77 \cr &r > 3.08 \end{aligned}
For integer $r$, $r > 3.08$ holds for all $r \ge 4$. Therefore, $\text{P}(X = r + 1) < \text{P}(X = r)$ for all $r \ge 4$.

(b)(iii) Mode and Exact Probability:

Evaluating the ratio at $r = 3$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{P}(X = 4)}{\text{P}(X = 3)} &= \dfrac{2(50 - 3)}{23(3 + 1)} \cr &= \dfrac{94}{92} \cr &> 1 \end{aligned}
Since $\text{P}(X = 4) > \text{P}(X = 3)$ and probabilities decrease strictly for all $r \ge 4$, the mode is $4$.

Calculating the exact binomial probability at the mode:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X = 4) \cr &\quad = \binom{50}{4}(0.08)^4 (0.92)^{46} \cr &\quad \approx 0.2037 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $0.672$, (b)(iii) Mode $= 4$, $\text{P}(X = 4) = 0.2037$

pi_options.feedback: Using the continuous standard Normal empirical rule $\text{P}(-1 < Z < 1) \approx 0.683$ ignores the discrete integer range and continuity correction.
Selecting $r = 3$ as the mode confuses the last index of the comparison step with the peak outcome at $r + 1 = 4$.
Using a Poisson approximation $\text{Po}(4)$ gives $\frac{4^4 e^{-4}}{4!} \approx 0.1954$ rather than computing the exact binomial probability.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Discreteness in Standard Deviation Intervals
bradley_insight.content: When asked for the probability of being within $1$ standard deviation of the mean for an approximated Binomial distribution, do not simply write down $0.683$. The random variable $Y$ is discrete. First calculate $(\mu - \sigma, \mu + \sigma) = (56.33, 71.67)$, identify the exact integer bounds $57 \le Y \le 71$, and only then apply continuity corrections to get $56.5$ and $71.5$.

question:
A local council monitors the journey times, $t$ in minutes, of cyclists using a cycle superhighway during the morning commute. The data have been grouped, and the frequency densities have been calculated to draw a histogram. Some of the data are presented in the table below:

Time, $t$ (mins)CyclistsFD
$10 \le t < 15$$18$$3.6$
$15 \le t < 20$$31$$A$
$20 \le t < 30$$74$$7.4$
$30 \le t < 40$$62$$6.2$
$40 \le t < 60$$B$$1.6$

(a) Calculate the missing values $A$ and $B$.

(b) An analyst labels the horizontal axis of the histogram 'Journey time in minutes' and the vertical axis 'Number of minutes per cyclist'.

State which one of these axis labels is incorrect and write down a correct version.
steps:
(a) Calculating the Missing Values $A$ and $B$:

Frequency density is defined as:\begin{aligned} \text{FD} &= \dfrac{\text{Frequency}}{\text{Class width}} \end{aligned}
For the class $15 \le t < 20$:\begin{aligned} \text{Width} &= 20 - 15 \cr &= 5 \cr A &= \dfrac{31}{5} \cr &= 6.2 \end{aligned}
For the class $40 \le t < 60$:\begin{aligned} \text{Width} &= 60 - 40 \cr &= 20 \cr B &= 20 \times 1.6 \cr &= 32 \end{aligned}

(b) Correcting the Axis Nomenclature:

The vertical axis label 'Number of minutes per cyclist' is incorrect.

The vertical axis represents frequency density, which has dimensions of frequency per unit of the continuous variable.

A correct label is Frequency density (or Number of cyclists per minute).
Final Answer: (a) $A = 6.2$, $B = 32$, (b) Vertical axis: Frequency density

pi_options.feedback: Dividing the frequency $31$ by the upper class boundary $20$ rather than the class width of $5$ gives $A = 1.55$.
Dividing the frequency density $1.6$ by the class width of $20$ rather than multiplying gives $B = 0.08$ instead of $32$.
The horizontal axis correctly represents the continuous variable (time in minutes); it is the vertical axis that was incorrectly labelled.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Units of Frequency Density
bradley_insight.content: Frequency density is calculated as $\frac{\text{Frequency}}{\text{Class width}}$. Its units are always frequency units per continuous variable unit, such as cyclists per minute. Writing minutes per cyclist inverts the ratio, which is a common conceptual slip on exam papers.

question:
The times taken, $t$ in minutes, for electric vehicles to recharge at a motorway service station are recorded. The grouped data and corresponding frequency densities are partially recorded in the table below:

Time, $t$ (mins)VehiclesFD
$0 \le t < 20$$28$$1.4$
$20 \le t < 30$$45$$P$
$30 \le t < 45$$Q$$4.8$
$45 \le t < 60$$51$$3.4$
$60 \le t < 90$$36$$1.2$

(a) Calculate the values of $P$ and $Q$.

(b) Use the data in the table to estimate the number of vehicles that had a charging time of at least $35$ minutes.

(c) State the modelling assumption about the distribution of charging times that you made in order to calculate your estimate in part (b).
steps:
(a) Calculating $P$ and $Q$:

For the class $20 \le t < 30$:\begin{aligned} \text{Width} &= 30 - 20 \cr &= 10 \cr P &= \dfrac{45}{10} \cr &= 4.5 \end{aligned}
For the class $30 \le t < 45$:\begin{aligned} \text{Width} &= 45 - 30 \cr &= 15 \cr Q &= 15 \times 4.8 \cr &= 72 \end{aligned}

(b) Estimating Vehicles Charging for at Least 35 Minutes:

The condition $t \ge 35$ spans part of the interval $30 \le t < 45$, and the entirety of the subsequent two intervals.

For the sub-interval $35 \le t < 45$:\begin{aligned} \text{Sub-width} &= 45 - 35 \cr &= 10 \cr f_{[35, 45)} &= 10 \times 4.8 \cr &= 48 \end{aligned}
Summing with the remaining complete classes:\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 48 + 51 + 36 \cr &= 135 \end{aligned}

(c) Identifying the Modelling Assumption:

To calculate the proportion of vehicles in $35 \le t < 45$, it is assumed that the charging times are distributed uniformly (evenly) across the class interval.
Final Answer: (a) $P = 4.5$, $Q = 72$, (b) $135$, (c) Uniform distribution across interval

pi_options.feedback: Calculating the lower sub-interval $35 - 30 = 5$ minutes gives $5 \times 4.8 = 24$, which incorrectly sums to $24 + 51 + 36 = 111$.
Linear interpolation within grouped continuous frequency classes assumes a uniform distribution, not a normal distribution.
Dividing the frequency $45$ by the upper class boundary $30$ rather than the class width $10$ incorrectly yields $P = 1.5$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Sub-Interval Frequency Estimation
bradley_insight.content: When estimating frequency for a partial class interval like $t \ge 35$ in $[30, 45)$, multiply the sub-interval width directly by the frequency density: $(45 - 35) \times 4.8 = 48$. This method avoids converting back and forth through total frequencies.

question:
The masses, $m$ in grams, of a harvest of fruit are summarised in the frequency table below:

Mass, $m$ (g)FreqFD
$80 \le m < 100$$30$$1.5$
$100 \le m < 110$$42$$4.2$
$110 \le m < 125$$63$$4.2$
$125 \le m < 150$$55$$2.2$
$150 \le m < 200$$40$$0.8$

A histogram is drawn on graph paper to represent these data. In this histogram, the bar representing the class $80 \le m < 100$ has a width of $4\text{ cm}$ and a height of $3\text{ cm}$.

(a) Find the width and the height, in cm, of the bar representing the class $110 \le m < 125$.

(b) Determine the number of pieces of fruit represented by an area of $1\text{ cm}^2$ on this histogram.

(c) On the same histogram, an additional class of fruit is drawn. The bar has a width of $5\text{ cm}$ and an area of $16\text{ cm}^2$. Determine the frequency of this class.
steps:
(a) Calculating Dimensions of the Bar:

For the reference class $80 \le m < 100$:\begin{aligned} \text{Class width} &= 100 - 80 \cr &= 20\text{ g} \end{aligned}
A class width of $20\text{ g}$ corresponds to $4\text{ cm}$:\begin{aligned} \text{Width scale} &= \dfrac{4\text{ cm}}{20\text{ g}} \cr &= 0.2\text{ cm per g} \end{aligned}
For $110 \le m < 125$, the class width is $15\text{ g}$:\begin{aligned} \text{Bar width} &= 15 \times 0.2 \cr &= 3\text{ cm} \end{aligned}
The frequency density of $1.5$ corresponds to $3\text{ cm}$:\begin{aligned} \text{Height scale} &= \dfrac{3\text{ cm}}{1.5} \cr &= 2\text{ cm per unit} \end{aligned}
For $110 \le m < 125$, the frequency density is $4.2$:\begin{aligned} \text{Bar height} &= 4.2 \times 2 \cr &= 8.4\text{ cm} \end{aligned}

(b) Frequency Represented by an Area of 1 cm²:

For the reference bar $80 \le m < 100$:\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 4\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} \cr &= 12\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}
This area represents a frequency of $30$ fruits:\begin{aligned} \text{Frequency per cm}^2 &= \dfrac{30}{12} \cr &= 2.5 \end{aligned}

(c) Finding Frequency from Given Area:

Using the established scaling factor of $2.5$ fruits per $\text{cm}^2$:\begin{aligned} \text{Frequency} &= 16 \times 2.5 \cr &= 40 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Width $= 3\text{ cm}$, Height $= 8.4\text{ cm}$, (b) $2.5$, (c) $40$

pi_options.feedback: Inverting the area-to-frequency ratio as $\frac{12}{30} = 0.4$ leads to $16 \times 0.4 = 6.4$ fruits.
Using the frequency density of $4.2$ directly as the bar height in cm ignores the vertical scale factor of $2\text{ cm}$ per unit.
Setting the bar width equal to the class width of $15$ ignores the horizontal scale factor of $0.2\text{ cm}$ per gram.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Area Proportionality Constant
bradley_insight.content: In histograms, $\text{Frequency} = k \times \text{Area}$. Find $k$ immediately from the given bar: $k = \frac{30}{12\text{ cm}^2} = 2.5\text{ items per cm}^2$. Once you have $k$, you can determine the frequency of any region directly from its area without calculating class boundaries.

question:
The speeds, $v$ in miles per hour (mph), of $160$ vehicles passing a speed camera on an urban road are summarised in the table below:

Speed, $v$ (mph)Frequency
$20 \le v < 30$$14$
$30 \le v < 36$$36$
$36 \le v < 40$$48$
$40 \le v < 48$$44$
$48 \le v < 60$$18$

(a) Write down the class interval that contains the median speed.

(b) Use linear interpolation to calculate an estimate of:
(i) the median speed;
(ii) the interquartile range (IQR) of the speeds.
Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

(c) The speed limit on this section of road is $40\text{ mph}$. Estimate the percentage of drivers who were exceeding the speed limit.
steps:
(a) Identifying the Median Class:

Find the cumulative frequencies:\begin{aligned} v &< 30: 14 \cr v &< 36: 14 + 36 = 50 \cr v &< 40: 50 + 48 = 98 \cr v &< 48: 98 + 44 = 142 \cr v &< 60: 142 + 18 = 160 \end{aligned}
The median position for $n = 160$ continuous values is $\frac{160}{2} = 80$.

Since $50 < 80 \le 98$, the median lies in $36 \le v < 40$.

(b)(i) Linear Interpolation for the Median:

Interpolating within $36 \le v < 40$:\begin{aligned} Q_2 &= 36 + \left(\dfrac{80 - 50}{48}\right) \times 4 \cr &= 36 + \left(\dfrac{30}{48}\right) \times 4 \cr &= 36 + 2.5 \cr &= 38.5\text{ mph} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Linear Interpolation for Quartiles and IQR:

Lower quartile position: $\frac{160}{4} = 40$ (in $30 \le v < 36$):\begin{aligned} Q_1 &= 30 + \left(\dfrac{40 - 14}{36}\right) \times 6 \cr &= 30 + \left(\dfrac{26}{36}\right) \times 6 \cr &= 30 + 4.333 \cr &= 34.333\text{ mph} \end{aligned}
Upper quartile position: $\frac{3(160)}{4} = 120$ (in $40 \le v < 48$):\begin{aligned} Q_3 &= 40 + \left(\dfrac{120 - 98}{44}\right) \times 8 \cr &= 40 + \left(\dfrac{22}{44}\right) \times 8 \cr &= 40 + 4 \cr &= 44.0\text{ mph} \end{aligned}
Evaluating the interquartile range:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= 44.0 - 34.333 \cr &= 9.667 \cr &\approx 9.7\text{ mph} \end{aligned}

(c) Estimating Percentage Exceeding the Speed Limit:

The number of drivers exceeding $40\text{ mph}$ is:\begin{aligned} \text{Exceeding} &= 44 + 18 \cr &= 62 \end{aligned}
Calculating the percentage of $160$ drivers:\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage} &= \left(\dfrac{62}{160}\right) \times 100\% \cr &= 38.75\% \cr &\approx 38.8\% \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $36 \le v < 40$, (b)(i) $38.5\text{ mph}$, (ii) $9.7\text{ mph}$, (c) $38.8\%

pi_options.feedback: Calculating the percentage of drivers obeying the limit ($\frac{98}{160} \times 100\% = 61.25\%$) rather than those exceeding it gives $61.3\%$.
Taking the midpoint of the median class $\frac{36 + 40}{2} = 38.0$ ignores linear interpolation within the frequency group.
Subtracting class midpoints ($44 - 33$) rather than interpolated quartiles gives $10.0$ instead of $9.7$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Continuous Data Quartile Positions
bradley_insight.content: For grouped continuous data, use exact fractional positions: $\frac{n}{2} = 80$, $\frac{n}{4} = 40$, and $\frac{3n}{4} = 120$. Do not use the discrete formulas $\frac{n + 1}{2}$ or $\frac{n + 1}{4}$ when carrying out linear interpolation on grouped continuous tables.

question:
The daily rainfall, $r$ in millimetres, was recorded at an environmental monitoring station over a period of $120$ days during autumn. The results are shown in the table below:

Rainfall, $r$ (mm)DaysFD
$0 \le r < 5$$45$$9.0$

$35 \le r < 60$$4$$0.16$

For these data, linear interpolation gives the lower quartile as $Q_1 = 3.3\text{ mm}$ and the upper quartile as $Q_3 = 14.2\text{ mm}$.

(a)
(i) Calculate the interquartile range (IQR) of the daily rainfall.
(ii) An outlier is defined as any value that exceeds $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$. Calculate the outlier boundary and explain whether any of the recorded days are definitely outliers.

(b) Use linear interpolation to calculate an estimate of the median daily rainfall, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.

(c) The mean daily rainfall for these $120$ days is $8.7\text{ mm}$. By comparing the mean and your estimated median, describe the skewness of the distribution, giving a reason for your answer.
steps:
(a)(i) Calculating the Interquartile Range:

Using the provided quartiles:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= Q_3 - Q_1 \cr &= 14.2 - 3.3 \cr &= 10.9\text{ mm} \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Outlier Boundary and Identification:

Evaluating the upper outlier threshold:\begin{aligned} \text{Boundary} &= Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR} \cr &= 14.2 + 1.5(10.9) \cr &= 14.2 + 16.35 \cr &= 30.55\text{ mm} \end{aligned}
The highest class interval $35 \le r < 60$ contains $4$ days. Because every observation in this class satisfies $r \ge 35 > 30.55\text{ mm}$, all $4$ of these days are definitely outliers.

(b) Linear Interpolation for the Median:

The median position for $n = 120$ observations is $\frac{120}{2} = 60$.

Cumulative frequency up to $r = 5$ is $45$, so the median lies in $5 \le r < 10$:\begin{aligned} \text{Median} &= 5 + \left(\dfrac{60 - 45}{35}\right) \times 5 \cr &= 5 + \left(\dfrac{15}{35}\right) \times 5 \cr &= 5 + \dfrac{15}{7} \cr &= 5 + 2.143 \cr &= 7.1\text{ mm} \end{aligned}

(c) Skewness Analysis:

Comparing the measures of central tendency:\begin{aligned} \text{Mean} &= 8.7\text{ mm} \cr \text{Median} &= 7.1\text{ mm} \cr \text{Mean} &> \text{Median} \end{aligned}
Because $\text{Mean} > \text{Median}$, the distribution is positively skewed (skewed to the right). The extreme high-rainfall outliers pull the mean above the median.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $10.9\text{ mm}$, (ii) $30.55\text{ mm}$, outliers exist, (b) $7.1\text{ mm}$, (c) Positively skewed

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Skewness and Measures of Location
bradley_insight.content: In a positively skewed distribution, the tail stretches to the right. The mode sits under the main peak, the median is pulled slightly right, and the mean is pulled farthest by extreme high values: $\text{Mode} < \text{Median} < \text{Mean}$.
