question:
The probability distribution of the discrete random variable $Y$ is given in the table below:

$y$$\text{P}(Y = y)$
$1$$0.1$
$2$$0.25$
$3$$k$
$4$$0.2$
$5$$0.15$

(a) Find the value of $k$.

$Y_1$ and $Y_2$ are two independent observations of $Y$.

(b) Find $\text{P}(Y_1 + Y_2 = 7)$.
steps:
(a) Finding the Value of $k$:

The sum of all probabilities in a discrete probability distribution must equal $1$:\begin{aligned} \sum \text{P}(Y = y) &= 1 \cr 0.1 + 0.25 + k \cr \quad + 0.2 + 0.15 &= 1 \cr 0.7 + k &= 1 \cr k &= 0.3 \end{aligned}

(b) Finding $\text{P}(Y_1 + Y_2 = 7)$:

Identify all pairs $(y_1, y_2)$ that sum to $7$ from the support $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$:
$$(2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2)$$
Since $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ are independent, multiply the respective probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(2, 5) &= 0.25 \times 0.15 \cr &= 0.0375 \cr \text{P}(3, 4) &= 0.3 \times 0.2 \cr &= 0.06 \cr \text{P}(4, 3) &= 0.2 \times 0.3 \cr &= 0.06 \cr \text{P}(5, 2) &= 0.15 \times 0.25 \cr &= 0.0375 \end{aligned}
Summing these mutually exclusive events:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(Y_1 + Y_2 = 7) \cr &\quad = 2(0.0375) + 2(0.06) \cr &\quad = 0.075 + 0.12 \cr &\quad = 0.195 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $k = 0.3$, (b) $0.195$

pi_options.feedback: Failing to account for the order of observations by calculating only $(2, 5)$ and $(3, 4)$ halves the correct probability.
An arithmetic error when summing the known probabilities to $0.6$ rather than $0.7$ gives $k = 0.4$.
Omitting one pair such as $(4, 3)$ from the sum of mutually exclusive outcomes gives $0.1575$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Order Matters in Independent Pairs
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating the sum of two independent observations, $(2, 5)$ and $(5, 2)$ represent distinct events: $Y_1 = 2, Y_2 = 5$ versus $Y_1 = 5, Y_2 = 2$. Always check whether pairs with distinct values need to be counted twice to avoid losing half your probability.

question:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the probability distribution shown in the table below, where $p$ and $q$ are constants:

$x$$\text{P}(X = x)$
$0$$0.15$
$1$$p$
$2$$0.2$
$3$$q$
$4$$0.1$

It is given that $\text{P}(X \le 1) = 0.35$.

(a) Find the values of $p$ and $q$.

$X_1$ and $X_2$ are two independent observations of $X$.

(b) Find the probability that $X_1 = X_2$.
steps:
(a) Determining the Unknowns $p$ and $q$:

Using the given cumulative probability $\text{P}(X \le 1) = 0.35$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 0) + \text{P}(X = 1) &= 0.35 \cr 0.15 + p &= 0.35 \cr p &= 0.2 \end{aligned}
Using the fact that all probabilities sum to $1$:\begin{aligned} \sum \text{P}(X = x) &= 1 \cr 0.15 + 0.2 + 0.2 \cr \quad + q + 0.1 &= 1 \cr 0.65 + q &= 1 \cr q &= 0.35 \end{aligned}

(b) Finding the Probability $\text{P}(X_1 = X_2)$:

Because $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent, the probability that both observations are equal is:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X_1 = X_2) \cr &\quad = \sum [\text{P}(X = x)]^2 \end{aligned}
Squaring the individual probabilities:\begin{aligned} 0.15^2 &= 0.0225 \cr 0.2^2 &= 0.04 \cr 0.2^2 &= 0.04 \cr 0.35^2 &= 0.1225 \cr 0.1^2 &= 0.01 \end{aligned}
Summing these values:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X_1 = X_2) \cr &\quad = 0.0225 + 0.04 \cr &\qquad + 0.04 + 0.1225 \cr &\qquad + 0.01 \cr &\quad = 0.235 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Doubling the squared terms inappropriately assumes that identical pairs like $(1, 1)$ must be counted twice.
Swapping the values of $p$ and $q$ ignores the equation $\text{P}(X = 0) + p = 0.35$.
Omitting the boundary terms $X = 0$ and $X = 4$ when calculating the sum of squares yields $0.200$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Sum of Squared Probabilities
bradley_insight.content: For two independent observations from the same discrete distribution, the event $X_1 = X_2$ corresponds to the main diagonal of the sample space table. It is always evaluated as $\sum [\text{P}(X = x)]^2$. Each diagonal entry appears exactly once.

question:
The discrete random variable $X$ has probability mass function defined by:
$$\text{P}(X = x) = cx$$ $$\text{for } x \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$$
where $c$ is a positive constant.

(a) Show that $c = 0.1$.

$X_1$ and $X_2$ are two independent observations of $X$.

(b) Find:
(i) $\text{P}(X_1 X_2 = 6)$
(ii) $\text{P}(X_1 > X_2)$
steps:
(a) Showing that $c = 0.1$:

The probabilities must sum to $1$ over the support $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$:\begin{aligned} \sum_{x=1}^4 \text{P}(X = x) &= 1 \cr c(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) &= 1 \cr 10c &= 1 \cr c &= 0.1 \end{aligned}
The distribution of $X$ is therefore:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 1) &= 0.1 \cr \text{P}(X = 2) &= 0.2 \cr \text{P}(X = 3) &= 0.3 \cr \text{P}(X = 4) &= 0.4 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Evaluating $\text{P}(X_1 X_2 = 6)$:

Pairs with a product of $6$ are $(2, 3)$ and $(3, 2)$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(2, 3) &= 0.2 \times 0.3 \cr &= 0.06 \cr \text{P}(3, 2) &= 0.3 \times 0.2 \cr &= 0.06 \end{aligned}
Summing these outcomes:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X_1 X_2 = 6) &= 0.06 + 0.06 \cr &= 0.12 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Evaluating $\text{P}(X_1 > X_2)$:

List the pairs where $X_1 > X_2$ by conditioning on $X_1$:\begin{aligned} X_1 = 2&: (2, 1) \cr X_1 = 3&: (3, 1), (3, 2) \cr X_1 = 4&: (4, 1), (4, 2), (4, 3) \end{aligned}
Calculate the probability for each value of $X_1$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X_1 = 2, X_2 < 2) &= 0.2(0.1) \cr &= 0.02 \cr \text{P}(X_1 = 3, X_2 < 3) &= 0.3(0.1 + 0.2) \cr &= 0.09 \cr \text{P}(X_1 = 4, X_2 < 4) &= 0.4(0.1 \cr & \quad + 0.2 + 0.3) \cr &= 0.24 \end{aligned}
Summing these mutually exclusive cases:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X_1 > X_2) &= 0.02 + 0.09 \cr &\quad + 0.24 \cr &= 0.35 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b)(i) $0.12$, (ii) $0.35$

pi_options.feedback: Counting only the pair $(2, 3)$ and omitting $(3, 2)$ overlooks that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are distinct independent observations.
Calculating $1 - \text{P}(X_1 = X_2) = 0.70$ gives $\text{P}(X_1 \neq X_2)$ rather than dividing by $2$ for $\text{P}(X_1 > X_2)$.
Evaluating the probability of identical pairs $\text{P}(X_1 = X_2) = 0.30$ confuses the equality event with the strict inequality event.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Symmetry Shortcuts for Inequalities
bradley_insight.content:
For two independent observations from an identical distribution, symmetry dictates that $\text{P}(X_1 > X_2) = \text{P}(X_2 > X_1)$.

Since:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X_1 > X_2) \cr &\quad + \text{P}(X_1 < X_2) \cr &\quad + \text{P}(X_1 = X_2) = 1 \end{aligned}you can quickly calculate $\text{P}(X_1 > X_2) = \dfrac{1 - \text{P}(X_1 = X_2)}{2}$.

With:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X_1 = X_2) \cr &\quad = 0.01 + 0.04 \cr &\qquad + 0.09 + 0.16 \cr &\quad = 0.30 \end{aligned}we get $\dfrac{1 - 0.30}{2} = 0.35$.

question:
The discrete random variable $W$ takes integer values from $-2$ to $2$. Its probability distribution is shown in the table below:

$w$$\text{P}(W = w)$
$-2$$0.1$
$-1$$0.25$
$0$$0.3$
$1$$a$
$2$$0.15$

(a) Find the value of $a$.

$W_1$ and $W_2$ are two independent observations of $W$.

(b) Find $\text{P}(W_1 + W_2 = 0)$.

(c) Find the conditional probability $\text{P}(W_1 + W_2 = 0 \mid W_1 > 0)$, giving your answer as an exact fraction in simplest form.
steps:
(a) Finding the Value of $a$:

Sum of probabilities must equal $1$:\begin{aligned} \sum \text{P}(W = w) &= 1 \cr 0.1 + 0.25 + 0.3 \cr \quad + a + 0.15 &= 1 \cr 0.8 + a &= 1 \cr a &= 0.2 \end{aligned}

(b) Evaluating $\text{P}(W_1 + W_2 = 0)$:

Identify pairs $(w_1, w_2)$ summing to $0$:
$$(-2, 2), (-1, 1), (0, 0),$$ $$(1, -1), (2, -2)$$
Calculate probabilities for each pair:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(-2, 2) &= 0.1 \times 0.15 \cr &= 0.015 \cr \text{P}(-1, 1) &= 0.25 \times 0.2 \cr &= 0.05 \cr \text{P}(0, 0) &= 0.3 \times 0.3 \cr &= 0.09 \cr \text{P}(1, -1) &= 0.2 \times 0.25 \cr &= 0.05 \cr \text{P}(2, -2) &= 0.15 \times 0.1 \cr &= 0.015 \end{aligned}
Summing these mutually exclusive events:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W_1 + W_2 = 0) \cr &\quad = 2(0.015) + 2(0.05) \cr &\qquad + 0.09 \cr &\quad = 0.03 + 0.1 + 0.09 \cr &\quad = 0.22 \end{aligned}

(c) Finding the Conditional Probability:

By definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W_1 + W_2 = 0 \mid W_1 > 0) \cr & = \dfrac{\text{P}((W_1 + W_2 = 0) \cap (W_1 > 0))}{\text{P}(W_1 > 0)} \end{aligned}
The condition $W_1 > 0$ means $W_1 \in \{1, 2\}$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W_1 > 0)\cr & \quad= \text{P}(W = 1) + \text{P}(W = 2) \cr &\quad= 0.2 + 0.15 \cr & \quad= 0.35 \end{aligned}
The intersection contains pairs where $w_1 + w_2 = 0$ and $w_1 > 0$:\begin{aligned} (1, -1)&: 0.2 \times 0.25 = 0.05 \cr (2, -2)&: 0.15 \times 0.1 = 0.015 \cr \text{Intersection} &= 0.05 + 0.015 \cr &= 0.065 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the ratio:\begin{aligned} \text{P} &= \dfrac{0.065}{0.35} \cr &= \dfrac{65}{350} \cr &= \dfrac{13}{70} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Conditioning on the sum being zero rather than $W_1 > 0$ evaluates $\frac{0.065}{0.22} = \frac{13}{44}$.
Forgetting the pair $(0, 0)$ when calculating the sum gives $0.22 - 0.09 = 0.13$ in part (b).
Counting only $(1, -1)$ in the intersection gives $\frac{0.05}{0.35} = \frac{1}{7}$, missing the pair $(2, -2)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Zero Sums Include (0, 0)
bradley_insight.content: When finding pairs summing to zero, candidates often pair up positives with negatives like $(-2, 2)$ and $(-1, 1)$, but completely forget $(0, 0)$. When $0$ is in the support, $0 + 0 = 0$ is a valid outcome that must be included.

question:
The discrete random variable $T$ has the probability distribution given in the table below:

$t$$\text{P}(T = t)$
$1$$\dfrac{1}{6}$
$2$$\dfrac{1}{3}$
$3$$\dfrac{1}{4}$
$4$$k$

(a) Find the value of $k$ as an exact fraction.

$T_1$ and $T_2$ are two independent observations of $T$.

(b) Find the probability that $|T_1 - T_2| = 1$. Give your answer as an irreducible fraction.

(c) Find $\text{P}(T_1 + T_2 \ge 6)$, giving your answer as an irreducible fraction.
steps:
(a) Finding $k$ as an Exact Fraction:

Total probability equals $1$:\begin{aligned} \sum \text{P}(T = t) &= 1 \cr \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{4} + k &= 1 \cr \dfrac{2 + 4 + 3}{12} + k &= 1 \cr \dfrac{9}{12} + k &= 1 \cr k &= \dfrac{3}{12} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}

(b) Finding $\text{P}(|T_1 - T_2| = 1)$:

Pairs where the absolute difference is $1$ are:
$$(1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3),$$ $$(3, 2), (3, 4), (4, 3)$$
Calculate probabilities for each unordered combination:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(1, 2) &= \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{18} \cr \text{P}(2, 3) &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{12} \cr \text{P}(3, 4) &= \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{16} \end{aligned}
Summing all ordered pairs:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(|T_1 - T_2| = 1) \cr &\quad = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{18}\right) + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{12}\right) \cr &\qquad + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{16}\right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{9} + \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{8} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{8 + 12 + 9}{72} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{29}{72} \end{aligned}

(c) Finding $\text{P}(T_1 + T_2 \ge 6)$:

Outcomes with sums $6$, $7$, or $8$:\begin{aligned} \text{Sum } 6&: (2, 4), (3, 3), (4, 2) \cr \text{Sum } 7&: (3, 4), (4, 3) \cr \text{Sum } 8&: (4, 4) \end{aligned}
Evaluating the probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(2, 4) + \text{P}(4, 2) &= 2\left(\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{4}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{6} \cr \text{P}(3, 3) &= \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2 \cr &= \dfrac{1}{16} \cr \text{P}(3, 4) + \text{P}(4, 3) &= 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{4}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{8} \cr \text{P}(4, 4) &= \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2 \cr &= \dfrac{1}{16} \end{aligned}
Summing these components:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(T_1 + T_2 \ge 6) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{16} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{16} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{4} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2 + 3}{12} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5}{12} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $k = \dfrac{1}{4}$, (b) $\dfrac{29}{72}$, (c) $\dfrac{5}{12}$

pi_options.feedback: Omitting the factor of $2$ for ordered pairs in part (b) results in $\frac{1}{18} + \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{16} = \frac{29}{144}$.
Forgetting the maximum outcome $(4, 4)$ when summing to at least $6$ yields $\frac{5}{12} - \frac{1}{16} = \frac{17}{48}$ or $\frac{3}{8}$.
An arithmetic error when adding the fractions leads to $1 - \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$ instead of $\frac{1}{4}$ for $k$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Systematic Summation of Fractions
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating sums of independent observations with fractional probabilities, group identical terms before converting to a common denominator: $2\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$. Grouping powers of $2$ reduces large denominators and prevents arithmetic errors.

question:
Jack and Oliver each wear a fitness tracker that records the number of steps they take per day. The daily results for a 7-day period are shown in the table below:

DayJackOliver
1$8450$$7850$
2$9210$$8420$
3$8860$$8190$
4$9580$$8760$
5$8940$$8950$
6$9340$$7630$
7$9320$$9350$

The 7-day mean is defined as the mean number of steps taken over the last 7 days. The 7-day mean for Jack is $9100$.

(a) Calculate the 7-day mean for Oliver.

At the end of day 8, a new 7-day mean is calculated for each person by including the number of steps taken on day 8 and omitting the number of steps taken on day 1. On day 8, Jack takes $9500$ steps.

(b) Determine the number of steps Oliver must take on day 8 so that his new 7-day mean at the end of day 8 is identical to Jack's new 7-day mean.

Over a long period of monitoring, Oliver's daily step count has a mean of $8800$ and a standard deviation of $920$.

(c) Determine whether the number of steps Oliver needs to take on day 8 found in part (b) is unusually high, using the criterion of being more than $2$ standard deviations above his long-term mean.
steps:
(a) Calculating Oliver's 7-Day Mean:

Sum Oliver's step counts for the 7 days:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total} \cr &\quad = 7850 \cr &\qquad + 8420 \cr &\qquad + 8190 \cr &\qquad + 8760 \cr &\qquad + 8950 \cr &\qquad + 7630 \cr &\qquad + 9350 \cr &\quad = 59\,150 \end{aligned}
Calculate the mean:\begin{aligned} &\text{Mean} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{59\,150}{7} \cr &\quad = 8450 \end{aligned}

(b) Updating Rolling Means for Day 8:

Find Jack's initial total steps:\begin{aligned} &\text{Jack Total} \cr &\quad = 7 \times 9100 \cr &\quad = 63\,700 \end{aligned}
Calculate Jack's new total for days 2 to 8:\begin{aligned} &\text{New Total} \cr &\quad = 63\,700 \cr &\qquad - 8450 \cr &\qquad + 9500 \cr &\quad = 64\,750 \end{aligned}
For Oliver to have the same 7-day mean, his total for days 2 to 8 must also equal $64\,750$.

Calculate Oliver's sum for days 2 to 7:\begin{aligned} &\text{Days 2 to 7} \cr &\quad = 59\,150 \cr &\qquad - 7850 \cr &\quad = 51\,300 \end{aligned}
Find Oliver's required steps on day 8:\begin{aligned} &\text{Day 8 Steps} \cr &\quad = 64\,750 \cr &\qquad - 51\,300 \cr &\quad = 13\,450 \end{aligned}

(c) Testing for an Unusually High Value:

Calculate the threshold of $2$ standard deviations above Oliver's long-term mean:\begin{aligned} &\text{Threshold} \cr &\quad = 8800 \cr &\qquad + 2(920) \cr &\quad = 8800 \cr &\qquad + 1840 \cr &\quad = 10\,640 \end{aligned}
Compare the required day 8 step count:\begin{aligned} 13\,450 > 10\,640 \end{aligned}
Because $13\,450$ exceeds this threshold, the number of steps is unusually high.
Final Answer: (a) $8450$, (b) $13\,450$, (c) Unusually high

pi_options.feedback: Subtracting Jack's day 1 value rather than Oliver's day 1 value of $7850$ gives $12\,650$.
Comparing against $3$ standard deviations ($8800 + 2760 = 11\,560$) or inverting the comparison incorrectly concludes it is not unusually high.
Adding day 1 rather than subtracting it when updating the 7-day window gives $14\,250$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Updating Moving Totals Efficiently
bradley_insight.content: When updating a moving average, you do not need to re-add all the intermediate days. The new total is always:\begin{aligned} &\text{New Total} \cr &\quad = \text{Old Total} \cr &\qquad - \text{Oldest Day} \cr &\qquad + \text{Newest Day} \end{aligned}Working with totals rather than means eliminates rounding errors.

question:
A local coffee shop records the number of customers served each weekday during a 5-day working week (Monday to Friday):

DayCustomers
Mon$142$
Tue$158$
Wed$165$
Thu$149$
Fri$186$

(a) Calculate the 5-day mean number of customers for this working week.

At the end of Saturday (Day 6), a new 5-day rolling mean is calculated by including Saturday's customer count and omitting Monday's count. The manager wishes the new 5-day rolling mean to represent a $5\%$ increase compared to the Monday–Friday mean.

(b) Determine the number of customers that must be served on Saturday to achieve this target.

Historic records show that Saturday customer numbers have a mean of $155$ and a standard deviation of $12$.

(c) Determine whether the required number of customers on Saturday found in part (b) is an outlier, defined as any value lying more than $2$ standard deviations from the historic Saturday mean.
steps:
(a) Calculating the Initial 5-Day Mean:

Sum the customer counts from Monday to Friday:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total} \cr &\quad = 142 \cr &\qquad + 158 \cr &\qquad + 165 \cr &\qquad + 149 \cr &\qquad + 186 \cr &\quad = 800 \end{aligned}
Calculate the mean:\begin{aligned} &\text{Mean} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{800}{5} \cr &\quad = 160 \end{aligned}

(b) Finding the Required Saturday Count:

Calculate the target 5-day mean with a $5\%$ increase:\begin{aligned} &\text{Target Mean} \cr &\quad = 160 \times 1.05 \cr &\quad = 168 \end{aligned}
Find the required total for the new 5-day window:\begin{aligned} &\text{New Total} \cr &\quad = 168 \times 5 \cr &\quad = 840 \end{aligned}
Calculate the sum for Tuesday to Friday:\begin{aligned} &\text{Tue to Fri} \cr &\quad = 800 - 142 \cr &\quad = 658 \end{aligned}
Determine Saturday's required count:\begin{aligned} &\text{Saturday} \cr &\quad = 840 - 658 \cr &\quad = 182 \end{aligned}

(c) Testing Saturday for Outlier Status:

Calculate the upper outlier boundary for historic Saturday counts:\begin{aligned} &\text{Upper Bound} \cr &\quad = 155 \cr &\qquad + 2(12) \cr &\quad = 155 + 24 \cr &\quad = 179 \end{aligned}
Compare Saturday's count:\begin{aligned} 182 > 179 \end{aligned}
Because $182$ exceeds the upper limit of $179$, it is classified as an outlier.
Final Answer: (a) $160$, (b) $182$, (c) Outlier

pi_options.feedback: Applying the $5\%$ increase directly to Saturday's historic mean rather than the rolling weekday mean gives $174$.
Testing against $3$ standard deviations ($155 + 36 = 191$) rather than the specified $2$ standard deviations incorrectly concludes it is not an outlier.
Forgetting to omit Monday's count from the total window calculation yields $840 - 644 = 196$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Percentage Change on Rolling Means
bradley_insight.content: A $5\%$ increase on a 5-day mean increases the total sum by $5 \times (160 \times 0.05) = 40$. Since the new day replaces an old day, the change in the total is simply:\begin{aligned} &\text{New Day} - \text{Old Day} \cr &\quad = 40 \end{aligned}Hence Saturday must be $142 + 40 = 182$.

question:
A manufacturing facility records its peak daily electrical power demand, $x$ in megawatts (MW), over a 7-day period. To simplify calculations, the data are coded using $y = x - 400$. The recorded values are given below:

Day$x$ (MW)$y$
1$412$$12$
2$408$$8$
3$415$$15$
4$395$$-5$
5$402$$2$
6$410$$10$
7$407$$7$

(a)
(i) Calculate the mean of the coded values, $\bar{y}$.
(ii) Hence find the mean peak power demand, $\bar{x}$, for the 7-day period.

At the end of day 8, a new 7-day rolling mean is calculated by including day 8 and omitting day 1. The factory manager requires the new 7-day mean peak demand to be $410\text{ MW}$.

(b) Calculate the peak power demand required on day 8 to achieve this rolling mean.

Historical records indicate that the daily peak power demand has a mean of $405\text{ MW}$ and a standard deviation of $10\text{ MW}$.

(c) Calculate the $z$-score for the day 8 power demand found in part (b), and state whether this demand represents an anomalous reading.
steps:
(a)(i) Calculating the Coded Mean $\bar{y}$:

Sum the coded values:\begin{aligned} &\sum y \cr &\quad = 12 + 8 \cr &\qquad + 15 - 5 \cr &\qquad + 2 + 10 \cr &\qquad + 7 \cr &\quad = 49 \end{aligned}
Calculate $\bar{y}$:\begin{aligned} &\bar{y} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{49}{7} \cr &\quad = 7 \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Finding the Uncoded Mean $\bar{x}$:

Using the coding relation $\bar{x} = \bar{y} + 400$:\begin{aligned} &\bar{x} \cr &\quad = 7 + 400 \cr &\quad = 407\text{ MW} \end{aligned}

(b) Finding the Required Power Demand on Day 8:

Calculate the initial 7-day total for $x$:\begin{aligned} &\text{Initial Total} \cr &\quad = 407 \times 7 \cr &\quad = 2849 \end{aligned}
Calculate the target total for the new 7-day window:\begin{aligned} &\text{New Total} \cr &\quad = 410 \times 7 \cr &\quad = 2870 \end{aligned}
Subtract day 1 demand from the initial total:\begin{aligned} &\text{Days 2 to 7} \cr &\quad = 2849 - 412 \cr &\quad = 2437 \end{aligned}
Determine day 8 demand:\begin{aligned} &\text{Day 8 Demand} \cr &\quad = 2870 - 2437 \cr &\quad = 433\text{ MW} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculating the $z$-Score and Checking for Anomaly:

Calculate the standardised $z$-score:\begin{aligned} &z \cr &\quad = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{433 - 405}{10} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{28}{10} \cr &\quad = 2.8 \end{aligned}
Because $|z| = 2.8 > 2$, the demand lies more than $2$ standard deviations from the historic mean and represents an anomalous reading.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $7$, (ii) $407\text{ MW}$, (b) $433\text{ MW}$, (c) $z = 2.8$, anomalous

pi_options.feedback: Using an incorrect standard deviation of $20$ rather than $10$ gives $z = 1.4$.
Omitting day 7 instead of day 1 when updating the window yields $421\text{ MW}$ and $z = 1.6$.
Subtracting the coded mean from $400$ instead of adding it incorrectly gives $\bar{x} = 393\text{ MW}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Linear Coding Rules
bradley_insight.content: For a linear code $y = \frac{x - a}{b}$, the mean transforms directly according to the formula:\begin{aligned} &\bar{y} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\bar{x} - a}{b} \end{aligned}However, the standard deviation is affected only by the scale factor $b$ and is independent of the shift $a$.

question:
A logistics warehouse records the time taken, $t$ in minutes, to dispatch priority parcels across $7$ consecutive shifts. The initial summary statistics for the $7$ shifts are:
$$\sum t = 1400 \quad \text{and}$$ $$\sum t^2 = 281\,400$$
(a) Calculate:
(i) the mean dispatch time, $\bar{t}$;
(ii) the standard deviation of the dispatch times, correct to 2 decimal places.

At the end of shift 8, a new 7-shift rolling statistic is computed by omitting shift 1 (where $t = 190\text{ minutes}$) and including shift 8 (where $t = 211\text{ minutes}$).

(b) Calculate for the new 7-shift period:
(i) the updated mean dispatch time;
(ii) the updated standard deviation, correct to 2 decimal places.

(c) State, with a reason, whether the dispatch times in the second 7-shift period were more consistent or less consistent than in the first 7-shift period.
steps:
(a)(i) Calculating the Initial Mean $\bar{t}$:

\begin{aligned} &\bar{t} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\sum t}{n} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1400}{7} \cr &\quad = 200\text{ mins} \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Calculating the Initial Standard Deviation:

Using the summary formula:\begin{aligned} &\sigma \cr &\quad = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum t^2}{n} - \bar{t}^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{\dfrac{281\,400}{7} - 200^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{40\,200 - 40\,000} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{200} \cr &\quad \approx 14.14\text{ mins} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Updating the Mean:

Update the sum of $t$ by removing shift 1 and adding shift 8:\begin{aligned} &\text{New } \sum t \cr &\quad = 1400 - 190 \cr &\qquad + 211 \cr &\quad = 1421 \end{aligned}
Calculate the updated mean:\begin{aligned} &\text{New Mean} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1421}{7} \cr &\quad = 203\text{ mins} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Updating the Standard Deviation:

Update the sum of squares:\begin{aligned} &190^2 = 36\,100 \cr &211^2 = 44\,521 \end{aligned}
\begin{aligned} &\text{New } \sum t^2 \cr &\quad = 281\,400 \cr &\qquad - 36\,100 \cr &\qquad + 44\,521 \cr &\quad = 289\,821 \end{aligned}
Calculate the new standard deviation:\begin{aligned} &\text{New } \sigma \cr &\quad = \sqrt{\dfrac{289\,821}{7} - 203^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{41\,403 - 41\,209} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{194} \cr &\quad \approx 13.93\text{ mins} \end{aligned}

(c) Evaluating Consistency:

Consistency is measured by the spread of the data.

Because the standard deviation decreased from $14.14\text{ mins}$ to $13.93\text{ mins}$, the dispatch times in the second 7-shift period were more consistent.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $200\text{ mins}$, (ii) $14.14\text{ mins}$, (b)(i) $203\text{ mins}$, (ii) $13.93\text{ mins}$, (c) More consistent

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $200\text{ mins}$, (ii) $14.14\text{ mins}$, (b)(i) $203\text{ mins}$, (ii) $13.93\text{ mins}$, (c) Less consistent
pi_options.feedback: Confusing an increase in the mean with an increase in variability incorrectly concludes the process is less consistent.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $200\text{ mins}$, (ii) $14.14\text{ mins}$, (b)(i) $203\text{ mins}$, (ii) $15.28\text{ mins}$, (c) Less consistent
pi_options.feedback: Adding $190^2$ and subtracting $211^2$ reverses the data modification and leads to an incorrect standard deviation of $15.28$.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $200\text{ mins}$, (ii) $15.28\text{ mins}$, (b)(i) $203\text{ mins}$, (ii) $13.93\text{ mins}$, (c) More consistent
pi_options.feedback: Dividing by $n - 1 = 6$ rather than $n = 7$ applies the sample standard deviation formula instead of the population formula.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Consistency Means Smaller Spread
bradley_insight.content: In examination questions, consistency refers strictly to measures of dispersion (standard deviation or interquartile range), never to the mean. A higher mean with a lower standard deviation represents faster or higher output with greater consistency.

question:
Two courier drivers, Driver A and Driver B, each record their delivery times (in minutes) for a standard delivery route on $7$ consecutive days. The times are shown below in ascending order:

Driver A:
$$38, \; 41, \; 42, \; 45,$$
$$46, \; 48, \; 62$$

Driver B:
$$40, \; 42, \; 43, \; 44,$$
$$45, \; 47, \; 49$$

(a) For Driver A:
(i) Find the median delivery time.
(ii) Find the lower quartile ($Q_1$) and upper quartile ($Q_3$).
(iii) Using the rule that an outlier is any value greater than $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, show that the delivery time of $62\text{ minutes}$ is an outlier.

(b) For Driver B, the median is $44\text{ minutes}$ and the interquartile range is $5\text{ minutes}$.

Compare the delivery times of Driver A and Driver B in context, referencing both an appropriate measure of central tendency and an appropriate measure of spread.
steps:
(a)(i) Finding the Median for Driver A:

For $n = 7$ ordered items, the median position is $\frac{7 + 1}{2} = 4$th value:\begin{aligned} &\text{Median} \cr &\quad = 45\text{ mins} \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Finding the Quartiles for Driver A:

The lower quartile position is $\frac{7 + 1}{4} = 2$nd value:\begin{aligned} &Q_1 \cr &\quad = 41\text{ mins} \end{aligned}
The upper quartile position is $\frac{3(7 + 1)}{4} = 6$th value:\begin{aligned} &Q_3 \cr &\quad = 48\text{ mins} \end{aligned}

(a)(iii) Demonstrating that 62 is an Outlier:

Calculate the interquartile range:\begin{aligned} &\text{IQR} \cr &\quad = Q_3 - Q_1 \cr &\quad = 48 - 41 \cr &\quad = 7\text{ mins} \end{aligned}
Calculate the upper outlier boundary:\begin{aligned} &\text{Upper Bound} \cr &\quad = Q_3 \cr &\qquad + 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &\quad = 48 \cr &\qquad + 1.5(7) \cr &\quad = 48 + 10.5 \cr &\quad = 58.5\text{ mins} \end{aligned}
Because $62 > 58.5$, the delivery time of $62\text{ minutes}$ is confirmed as an outlier.

(b) Comparative Analysis in Context:

Comparing central tendency (median):
Driver B's median of $44\text{ mins}$ is lower than Driver A's median of $45\text{ mins}$, indicating Driver B is generally faster on average.

Comparing spread (interquartile range):
Driver B's IQR of $5\text{ mins}$ is smaller than Driver A's IQR of $7\text{ mins}$, indicating Driver B has more consistent delivery times.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $45\text{ mins}$, (ii) $Q_1 = 41\text{ mins}$, $Q_3 = 48\text{ mins}$, (iii) $58.5\text{ mins}$, outlier, (b) Driver B faster and more consistent

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $45\text{ mins}$, (ii) $Q_1 = 41\text{ mins}$, $Q_3 = 48\text{ mins}$, (iii) $58.5\text{ mins}$, outlier, (b) Driver A faster and more consistent
pi_options.feedback: Inverting the comparisons incorrectly identifies Driver A as faster despite having a higher median of $45$ compared to $44$.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $45\text{ mins}$, (ii) $Q_1 = 41.5\text{ mins}$, $Q_3 = 47.5\text{ mins}$, (iii) $56.5\text{ mins}$, outlier, (b) Driver B faster and more consistent
pi_options.feedback: Interpolating between values rather than using the exact 2nd and 6th discrete ranks gives $Q_1 = 41.5$ and $Q_3 = 47.5$.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $45\text{ mins}$, (ii) $Q_1 = 41\text{ mins}$, $Q_3 = 48\text{ mins}$, (iii) $55.0\text{ mins}$, not an outlier, (b) Driver B faster and more consistent
pi_options.feedback: Using $1.0 \times \text{IQR}$ rather than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ calculates $48 + 7 = 55$ and incorrectly concludes $62$ is not an outlier.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Two-Part Contextual Comparison
bradley_insight.content: When asked to compare two distributions, you must always provide two separate statements with context and numerical support: one comparing a measure of central tendency (median or mean) and one comparing a measure of dispersion (IQR or standard deviation).

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A national survey reported that in January 2025, $58\%$ of households in a region subscribed to at least one streaming service. Later that year, an industry analyst believed that this proportion had increased. In November 2025, a random sample of $65$ households from the region was surveyed. It was found that $47$ of the $65$ households subscribed to at least one streaming service.

Use a suitable hypothesis test to determine whether there is evidence at the $1\%$ significance level to suggest that the proportion of households in the region subscribing to at least one streaming service had increased.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses and Distribution:

Let $p$ be the population proportion of households subscribing to at least one streaming service.

State the hypotheses:
$$H_0: p = 0.58$$
$$H_1: p > 0.58$$
Let $X$ be the number of households in the sample subscribing to a streaming service.

Under $H_0$, the test statistic follows:\begin{aligned} X \sim \text{B}(65, 0.58) \end{aligned}

(b) Calculating the Tail Probability:

The observed value is $X = 47$.

Calculate the upper tail probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \ge 47) \cr &\quad = 1 - \text{P}(X \le 46) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.9888 \cr &\quad = 0.0112 \end{aligned}

(c) Comparison and Conclusion:

Compare the $p$-value with the significance level $\alpha = 0.01$:\begin{aligned} 0.0112 > 0.01 \end{aligned}
Because $0.0112$ exceeds $0.01$, the result is not significant at the $1\%$ level.

Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence to suggest that the proportion of households subscribing to a streaming service has increased.
Final Answer: Do not reject $H_0$, insufficient evidence to suggest proportion has increased

pi_options.ans: Reject $H_0$, sufficient evidence to suggest proportion has increased
pi_options.feedback: Comparing against a $5\%$ level ($0.0112 < 0.05$) rather than the specified $1\%$ level incorrectly rejects $H_0$.

pi_options.ans: Do not reject $H_0$, sufficient evidence to suggest proportion has increased
pi_options.feedback: Failing to reject $H_0$ means there is insufficient evidence to support the claim in $H_1$.

pi_options.ans: Reject $H_0$, insufficient evidence to suggest proportion has increased
pi_options.feedback: Rejecting $H_0$ is contradictory to concluding that evidence is insufficient.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Significance Level Dictates Decision
bradley_insight.content: The observed count of $47$ is well above the expected mean:\begin{aligned} &65 \times 0.58 \cr &\quad = 37.7 \end{aligned}At the $5\%$ level ($p < 0.05$), this result would be significant. However, for a strict $1\%$ test, a probability of $0.0112$ is not quite rare enough to reject $H_0$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Historically, $35\%$ of patients diagnosed with a seasonal allergy at a medical clinic report persistent symptoms after receiving standard treatment. A doctor introduces a modified therapy programme and believes it reduces the proportion of patients reporting persistent symptoms.

In a clinical trial, a random sample of $40$ patients receives the modified therapy programme.

(a) State hypotheses to test the doctor's belief, defining any parameter used.

(b) Find the critical region for the test at the $5\%$ significance level.

(c) In the trial, $8$ patients report persistent symptoms. State the conclusion of the test in context.
steps:
(a) Stating the Hypotheses:

Let $p$ be the population proportion of patients reporting persistent symptoms.

The hypotheses are:
$$H_0: p = 0.35$$
$$H_1: p < 0.35$$

(b) Finding the Critical Region:

Let $X$ be the number of patients reporting persistent symptoms.

Under $H_0$:\begin{aligned} X \sim \text{B}(40, 0.35) \end{aligned}
Calculate lower tail probabilities near $5\%$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \le 8) \cr &\quad = 0.0303 \cr &\text{P}(X \le 9) \cr &\quad = 0.0644 \end{aligned}
Because $0.0303 < 0.05$ and $0.0644 > 0.05$, the critical region is:\begin{aligned} X \le 8 \end{aligned}

(c) Conclusion in Context:

The observed number of patients is $X = 8$.

Because $8$ lies within the critical region ($8 \le 8$), we reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $5\%$ level to suggest that the modified therapy programme reduces the proportion of patients with persistent symptoms.
Final Answer: (a) $H_0: p = 0.35$, $H_1: p < 0.35$, (b) $X \le 8$, (c) Reject $H_0$, evidence therapy reduces symptoms

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.35$, $H_1: p < 0.35$, (b) $X \le 9$, (c) Reject $H_0$, evidence therapy reduces symptoms
pi_options.feedback: Choosing $X \le 9$ as the critical region gives a tail probability of $0.0644$, which exceeds the $5\%$ significance level.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.35$, $H_1: p < 0.35$, (b) $X \le 8$, (c) Do not reject $H_0$, insufficient evidence of reduction
pi_options.feedback: Since the observed value $8$ falls directly inside the critical region $X \le 8$, $H_0$ must be rejected.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.35$, $H_1: p \neq 0.35$, (b) $X \le 8$, (c) Reject $H_0$, evidence therapy reduces symptoms
pi_options.feedback: The doctor specifically suspects a reduction in symptoms, which requires a one-tailed test ($p < 0.35$) rather than a two-tailed test.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Defining Parameters in Full
bradley_insight.content: Always define the parameter $p$ explicitly in words. Stating $H_0: p = 0.35$ without writing 'where $p$ is the proportion of patients reporting persistent symptoms' will forfeit an independent communication mark.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A quality control manager at a component factory knows that historically $8\%$ of manufactured electronic switches are non-conforming. Following the installation of a new assembly unit, the manager wishes to test at the $5\%$ level whether the proportion of non-conforming switches has changed.

A random sample of $50$ switches is tested.

(a) State the null and alternative hypotheses, defining the parameter $p$.

(b) Determine the critical region for this two-tailed test, ensuring the probability in each tail is as close to $2.5\%$ as possible without exceeding it.

(c) Calculate the actual significance level of the test.

(d) In the sample of $50$ switches, $8$ are found to be non-conforming. State the conclusion of the test in context.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

Let $p$ be the population proportion of non-conforming switches.

The hypotheses are:
$$H_0: p = 0.08$$
$$H_1: p \neq 0.08$$

(b) Finding the Critical Region:

Let $X$ be the number of non-conforming switches.

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(50, 0.08)$.

For a $5\%$ two-tailed test, allocate up to $2.5\%$ to each tail.

Lower tail:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \le 0) \cr &\quad = 0.0155 < 0.025 \cr &\text{P}(X \le 1) \cr &\quad = 0.0827 > 0.025 \end{aligned}
Lower critical region: $X = 0$.

Upper tail:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \ge 9) \cr &\quad = 1 - \text{P}(X \le 8) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.9818 \cr &\quad = 0.0182 < 0.025 \cr &\text{P}(X \ge 8) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.9510 \cr &\quad = 0.0490 > 0.025 \end{aligned}
Upper critical region: $X \ge 9$.

The overall critical region is:\begin{aligned} X = 0 \text{ or } X \ge 9 \end{aligned}

(c) Actual Significance Level:

Sum the probabilities of the two tails:\begin{aligned} &\text{Actual Level} \cr &\quad = 0.0155 \cr &\qquad + 0.0182 \cr &\quad = 0.0337 \cr &\quad = 3.37\% \end{aligned}

(d) Conclusion in Context:

The observed count is $X = 8$.

Because $8$ is not in the critical region ($1 \le 8 \le 8$), we do not reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to suggest that the proportion of non-conforming switches has changed.
Final Answer: (a) $H_0: p = 0.08$, $H_1: p \neq 0.08$, (b) $X = 0$ or $X \ge 9$, (c) $3.37\%$, (d) Insufficient evidence of change

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.08$, $H_1: p \neq 0.08$, (b) $X \le 1$ or $X \ge 8$, (c) $13.17\%$, (d) Insufficient evidence of change
pi_options.feedback: Using $X \le 1$ and $X \ge 8$ gives tail probabilities of $8.27\%$ and $4.90\%$, which exceed the $2.5\%$ limit per tail.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.08$, $H_1: p \neq 0.08$, (b) $X = 0$ or $X \ge 9$, (c) $5.00\%$, (d) Insufficient evidence of change
pi_options.feedback: Assuming the actual significance level equals the nominal $5\%$ level ignores the discrete nature of the binomial distribution.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.08$, $H_1: p \neq 0.08$, (b) $X = 0$ or $X \ge 9$, (c) $3.37\%$, (d) Reject $H_0$, evidence of change
pi_options.feedback: The observed value of $8$ lies outside the critical region ($X \ge 9$), so $H_0$ must not be rejected.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Nominal vs Actual Significance Levels
bradley_insight.content: Because the Binomial distribution is discrete, you cannot achieve an exact $5\%$ significance level. The actual significance level is the sum of the true probabilities in the critical region:\begin{aligned} &0.0155 + 0.0182 \cr &\quad = 0.0337 \end{aligned}This is strictly less than the nominal $5\%$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A seed merchant claims that the germination rate of a batch of wildflower seeds is $75\%$. A horticulturist suspects that the seeds have been stored in optimal conditions and that the germination rate is higher than claimed.

The horticulturist plants a random sample of $30$ seeds and counts the number of seeds, $X$, that successfully germinate.

(a) State suitable hypotheses for the test, defining the parameter $p$.

(b) Find the critical value for a test at the $5\%$ significance level.

(c) Given that $27$ seeds germinate:
(i) Calculate the $p$-value of this outcome.
(ii) State, with justification, whether the merchant's claim should be rejected at the $5\%$ level.

(d) State the probability of incorrectly rejecting the null hypothesis for this test.
steps:
(a) Stating the Hypotheses:

Let $p$ be the population proportion of seeds that germinate.

The hypotheses are:
$$H_0: p = 0.75$$
$$H_1: p > 0.75$$

(b) Finding the Critical Value:

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(30, 0.75)$.

Calculate upper tail probabilities:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \ge 27) \cr &\quad = 1 - \text{P}(X \le 26) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.9547 \cr &\quad = 0.0453 < 0.05 \cr &\text{P}(X \ge 26) \cr &\quad = 1 - \text{P}(X \le 25) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.8943 \cr &\quad = 0.1057 > 0.05 \end{aligned}
The critical region is $X \ge 27$, so the critical value is $27$.

(c)(i) Calculating the $p$-Value:

For $X = 27$, the $p$-value is the probability of obtaining at least $27$ germinated seeds under $H_0$:\begin{aligned} &p\text{-value} \cr &\quad = \text{P}(X \ge 27) \cr &\quad = 0.0453 \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Testing the Claim:

Compare the $p$-value with the significance level:\begin{aligned} 0.0453 < 0.05 \end{aligned}
Because $0.0453 < 0.05$ (and $27$ lies in the critical region), reject $H_0$.

There is sufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to suggest that the germination rate is higher than $75\%$.

(d) Probability of Incorrectly Rejecting $H_0$:

Incorrectly rejecting $H_0$ when it is true is a Type I error.

Its probability equals the actual significance level of the test:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(\text{Type I Error}) \cr &\quad = \text{P}(X \ge 27) \cr &\quad = 0.0453 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Selecting $26$ as the critical value yields a tail probability of $0.1057$, exceeding the $5\%$ threshold.
Since the $p$-value of $0.0453$ is strictly less than $0.05$, $H_0$ must be rejected.
The probability of incorrectly rejecting $H_0$ is the actual significance level ($0.0453$), not the nominal level of $0.0500$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Type I Error and Actual Level
bradley_insight.content: A Type I error is rejecting $H_0$ given that $H_0$ is true. This happens whenever the test statistic falls into the critical region under $H_0$. Therefore, the probability of a Type I error is always equal to the actual significance level, which is $0.0453$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

An online retailer knows from long-term records that $20\%$ of customer enquiries are resolved via its automated chatbot. The software is updated, and the customer service director claims that the update has increased the proportion of enquiries resolved by the chatbot.

To test this claim at the $2.5\%$ level of significance, a random sample of $45$ customer enquiries is monitored, and $15$ are successfully resolved by the chatbot.

(a) State two assumptions needed to model the number of resolved enquiries using a binomial distribution.

(b) Define the test statistic and state the hypotheses to test the director's claim.

(c) Carry out the hypothesis test at the $2.5\%$ significance level, stating your conclusion clearly in context.
steps:
(a) Binomial Assumptions in Context:

Two required modelling assumptions are:
1. Each enquiry is resolved independently of all other enquiries.
2. The probability of an enquiry being resolved remains constant for all enquiries.

(b) Defining Test Statistic and Hypotheses:

Let $X$ be the number of enquiries in the sample resolved by the chatbot.

Let $p$ be the population proportion of enquiries resolved by the chatbot.

The hypotheses are:
$$H_0: p = 0.2$$
$$H_1: p > 0.2$$

(c) Conducting the Test and Conclusion:

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(45, 0.2)$.

The observed number of resolved enquiries is $X = 15$.

Calculate the probability of obtaining at least $15$ resolved enquiries:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \ge 15) \cr &\quad = 1 - \text{P}(X \le 14) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.9774 \cr &\quad = 0.0226 \end{aligned}
Compare with the significance level $\alpha = 0.025$:\begin{aligned} 0.0226 < 0.025 \end{aligned}
Because $0.0226 < 0.025$, the result is significant at the $2.5\%$ level.

Reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence at the $2.5\%$ level to suggest that the update has increased the proportion of enquiries resolved by the chatbot.
Final Answer: (a) Independent enquiries, constant probability, (b) $X$, $H_0: p = 0.2$, $H_1: p > 0.2$, (c) Reject $H_0$, evidence proportion increased

pi_options.ans: (a) Independent enquiries, constant probability, (b) $X$, $H_0: p = 0.2$, $H_1: p > 0.2$, (c) Do not reject $H_0$, insufficient evidence of increase
pi_options.feedback: Because the tail probability of $0.0226$ is strictly less than $0.025$, the test is significant and $H_0$ must be rejected.

pi_options.ans: (a) Fixed sample size only, constant probability, (b) $X$, $H_0: p = 0.2$, $H_1: p = 0.25$, (c) Reject $H_0$, evidence proportion increased
pi_options.feedback: The alternative hypothesis must state a strict inequality ($p > 0.2$) rather than a specific numerical value.

pi_options.ans: (a) Independent enquiries, constant probability, (b) $X$, $H_0: p = 0.2$, $H_1: p < 0.2$, (c) Reject $H_0$, evidence proportion increased
pi_options.feedback: The director claims an increase in the resolution rate, so $H_1$ must be $p > 0.2$, not $p < 0.2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: State Assumptions in Context
bradley_insight.content: When asked for assumptions of a Binomial model, never just write 'independence and constant probability'. Always frame them in the context of the question: 'each enquiry is independent' and 'the probability of resolution is constant across enquiries'.

question:
A regional environmental agency maintains records on household recycling rates and annual residual landfill waste per household across local authority districts.

The diagram in Fig. 1.1 was generated using spreadsheet software and summarises the household recycling rates ($x\%$) for all districts in a northern metropolitan area.

(a) Identify two respects in which the presentation of the data in Fig. 1.1 is incorrect.

Fig. 1.2 in the same diagram shows a scatter diagram of annual residual landfill waste per household, $y$ in tonnes, against recycling rate, $x\%$, for a sample of $47$ districts in the region. A line of best fit has also been drawn. The equation of the line of best fit is:
$$y = -0.024x + 1.86$$
(b)
(i) What does the diagram suggest about the relationship between recycling rate and landfill waste?
(ii) In one district, the recycling rate is recorded as $38.5\%$, but the landfill waste figure was lost. Use the equation of the line of best fit to estimate the annual landfill waste per household for this district.
(iii) Explain why it would not be sensible to use this equation to estimate the landfill waste for a district where the recycling rate is $3.0\%$.
(iv) Explain why it would not be reliable to use this model to estimate the landfill waste in a rural district located in a southern county.
(v) Explain why it is unlikely that this sample of $47$ districts is a simple random sample from the metropolitan area.

(c) Across the metropolitan area, there are $48$ districts available on an alphabetical register. Describe how a sample of size $12$ could be selected using systematic sampling.
steps:
(a) Presentation Errors in Fig. 1.1:

Two errors in the spreadsheet chart are:
1. Equal bar widths are drawn even though the class intervals are unequal (some intervals have width $5$, others width $10$). The vertical axis should represent frequency density rather than frequency.
2. There are gaps between the bars, which is incorrect for continuous grouped data.

(b)(i) Relationship:

The scatter diagram shows a negative correlation (as the household recycling rate increases, the annual landfill waste per household tends to decrease).

(b)(ii) Estimating Landfill Waste:

Substitute $x = 38.5$ into the line of best fit:\begin{aligned} y &= -0.024(38.5) \cr &\quad + 1.86 \cr &= -0.924 + 1.86 \cr &= 0.936\text{ tonnes} \end{aligned}
The estimated landfill waste is $0.936\text{ tonnes}$ (or $0.94\text{ tonnes}$).

(b)(iii) Extrapolation:

A recycling rate of $3.0\%$ lies well below the minimum observed value in the sample ($x \approx 15\%$). Using the linear model outside the range of sample data represents extrapolation, and the relationship cannot be assumed to hold.

(b)(iv) Population Validity:

The model is calibrated specifically on northern metropolitan (urban) districts. Rural districts in the south may have differing waste collection policies, garden waste volumes, and demographic profiles, making the model unreliable for other regions.

(b)(v) Non-Random Nature of Sample:

With $47$ out of $48$ districts included, almost the entire population was taken. The omission of just one district was almost certainly caused by missing data (an opportunity sample) rather than a planned random selection.

(c) Systematic Sampling Method:

Calculate the sampling interval:\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{48}{12} \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}
1. Number the $48$ districts from $1$ to $48$ on the alphabetical register.
2. Generate a random integer between $1$ and $4$ inclusive as the starting district.
3. Select every $4$th district on the register thereafter (e.g. $r, r+4, r+8, \dots$).

Final Answer: (a) Equal bar widths for unequal classes, gaps between continuous bars, (b)(i) Negative correlation, (ii) $0.936\text{ tonnes}$, (iii) Extrapolation, (iv) Different demographic population, (v) Nearly whole population, (c) Interval $4$, random start from $1$ to $4$, select every $4$th

pi_options.ans: (a) Vertical axis has wrong scale, bars are too dark, (b)(i) Negative correlation, (ii) $0.936\text{ tonnes}$, (iii) Extrapolation, (iv) Different demographic population, (v) Nearly whole population, (c) Interval $4$, random start from $1$ to $4$, select every $4$th
pi_options.feedback: Shading and axis scaling are stylistic design choices, not mathematical errors for continuous grouped data.

pi_options.ans: (a) Equal bar widths for unequal classes, gaps between continuous bars, (b)(i) Negative correlation, (ii) $0.936\text{ tonnes}$, (iii) Interpolation, (iv) Different demographic population, (v) Nearly whole population, (c) Interval $12$, random start from $1$ to $12$, select every $12$th
pi_options.feedback: A recycling rate of $3.0\%$ is extrapolation outside the sample range ($x \ge 15\%$), and the interval is $48 / 12 = 4$, not $12$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Equal bar widths for unequal classes, gaps between continuous bars, (b)(i) Positive correlation, (ii) $2.784\text{ tonnes}$, (iii) Extrapolation, (iv) Different demographic population, (v) Nearly whole population, (c) Interval $4$, random start from $1$ to $4$, select every $4$th
pi_options.feedback: The gradient is negative ($-0.024$), indicating negative correlation, and adding $0.924$ instead of subtracting gives $2.784$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Spotting Histogram Spreadsheet Errors
bradley_insight.content: Standard spreadsheet software often defaults to drawing bar charts with equal bar widths and spaces even when given unequal class intervals. In a true histogram for continuous data, the area must be proportional to frequency, requiring frequency density on the vertical axis and touching bars.

question:
A student investigates weather records from a UK meteorological station using the Large Data Set. Fig. 2.1 shows a scatter diagram of daily total sunshine, $s$ in hours, against daily mean temperature, $t$ in $^\circ\text{C}$, for a sample of summer days.

The equation of the regression line of $s$ on $t$ is:
$$s = 0.45t - 1.20$$
(a) State the type of correlation shown by the scatter diagram.

(b) Point $P$ on the scatter diagram represents a day where $t = 19.0^\circ\text{C}$ and $s = 1.4\text{ hours}$. Point $P$ is an outlier. Suggest a plausible meteorological reason for this unusual observation.

(c) Use the regression equation to estimate the daily total sunshine for a day with a daily mean temperature of $16.0^\circ\text{C}$.

(d) Explain why it would not be sensible to use this regression equation to estimate the sunshine for a day when the mean temperature is $32.0^\circ\text{C}$.

(e) The student wishes to select a sample of size $15$ from a sampling frame of $180$ consecutive days from the meteorological records. Describe how systematic sampling could be used to select this sample.
steps:
(a) Type of Correlation:

The scatter diagram shows positive correlation (as daily mean temperature increases, daily total sunshine tends to increase).

(b) Plausible Meteorological Reason for Outlier $P$:

Point $P$ represents a warm day ($19.0^\circ\text{C}$) with very little sunshine ($1.4\text{ hours}$). A plausible explanation is that the day was warm but heavily overcast, humid, or covered by thick cloud.

(c) Estimating Daily Sunshine:

Substitute $t = 16.0$ into the regression line:\begin{aligned} s &= 0.45(16.0) \cr &\quad - 1.20 \cr &= 7.20 - 1.20 \cr &= 6.0\text{ hours} \end{aligned}

(d) Reliability of Estimation at $32.0^\circ$C:

The temperature $32.0^\circ\text{C}$ is well above the maximum recorded temperature in the sample ($t \approx 22^\circ\text{C}$). Making a prediction outside the range of observed data is extrapolation, and the linear relationship cannot be assumed to hold.

(e) Systematic Sampling Method:

Calculate the sampling interval:\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{180}{15} \cr &= 12 \end{aligned}
1. Number the days sequentially from $1$ to $180$.
2. Select a random number between $1$ and $12$ inclusive as the starting day.
3. Select every $12$th day thereafter (e.g. $r, r+12, r+24, \dots$).

Final Answer: (a) Positive correlation, (b) Warm and heavily overcast day, (c) $6.0\text{ hours}$, (d) Extrapolation beyond sample range, (e) Interval $12$, random start from $1$ to $12$, select every $12$th

pi_options.ans: (a) Positive correlation, (b) Instrument malfunction only, (c) $6.0\text{ hours}$, (d) Extrapolation beyond sample range, (e) Interval $15$, random start from $1$ to $15$, select every $15$th
pi_options.feedback: A meteorological explanation relates to atmospheric conditions (cloud cover), and the sampling interval is $180 / 15 = 12$, not $15$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Negative correlation, (b) Warm and heavily overcast day, (c) $6.0\text{ hours}$, (d) Extrapolation beyond sample range, (e) Interval $12$, random start from $1$ to $12$, select every $12$th
pi_options.feedback: The points rise from bottom-left to top-right with a positive gradient ($+0.45$), indicating positive correlation, not negative.

pi_options.ans: (a) Positive correlation, (b) Warm and heavily overcast day, (c) $8.4\text{ hours}$, (d) Interpolation within sample range, (e) Interval $12$, random start from $1$ to $12$, select every $12$th
pi_options.feedback: Adding $1.20$ instead of subtracting gives $7.20 + 1.20 = 8.4$, and $32^\circ\text{C}$ is an extrapolation, not an interpolation.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Identifying Contextual Causes for Outliers
bradley_insight.content: When asked for a reason for a bivariate weather outlier, examiners look for physical weather conditions rather than generic excuses like 'recording error'. A warm day with almost no sunshine represents a humid, overcast summer day.

question:
A transport researcher studies the relationship between engine size, $x$ in litres, and carbon dioxide emissions, $y$ in grams per kilometre ($\text{g/km}$), for a sample of passenger cars.

The least-squares regression line of $y$ on $x$ for the sample is:
$$y = 28.5x + 78.2$$
The values of engine size in the sample ranged from $1.0\text{ litre}$ to $3.5\text{ litres}$.

(a) Interpret in context:
(i) the gradient ($28.5$);
(ii) the intercept ($78.2$), commenting on its practical validity.

(b) Estimate the $\text{CO}_2$ emissions for a car with an engine size of $2.0\text{ litres}$.

(c) A car is known to produce $160\text{ g/km}$ of $\text{CO}_2$. Explain why it is statistically inappropriate to rearrange the given regression equation to estimate its engine size $x$.

(d) The researcher finds a strong positive correlation between engine size and $\text{CO}_2$ emissions. Explain whether this demonstrates that having a larger engine causes higher emissions.

(e) The sampling frame contains $600$ petrol cars, $300$ diesel cars, and $100$ hybrid cars. Explain how a stratified sample of size $40$ would be chosen, stating the number of cars of each fuel type required.
steps:
(a)(i) Interpreting the Gradient:

The gradient indicates that for every additional $1\text{ litre}$ increase in engine size, $\text{CO}_2$ emissions are estimated to increase by $28.5\text{ g/km}$.

(a)(ii) Interpreting the Intercept:

The intercept suggests that a car with an engine size of $0\text{ litres}$ would produce $78.2\text{ g/km}$ of $\text{CO}_2$. This has no practical validity because an engine cannot have zero volume, and $x = 0$ is an extrapolation outside the data range ($1.0 \le x \le 3.5$).

(b) Estimating Emissions:

Substitute $x = 2.0$ into the regression line:\begin{aligned} y &= 28.5(2.0) \cr &\quad + 78.2 \cr &= 57.0 + 78.2 \cr &= 135.2\text{ g/km} \end{aligned}

(c) Non-Reversibility of the Regression Line:

The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is constructed by minimising the sum of squared vertical residuals in $y$, assuming $x$ is the independent variable. To estimate $x$ from $y$, a separate regression line of $x$ on $y$ (minimising horizontal residuals) must be calculated.

(d) Correlation versus Causation:

No. Correlation does not imply causation. While there is a strong association, higher emissions could be caused by confounding variables correlated with engine size, such as total vehicle mass or fuel consumption rate.

(e) Stratified Sampling Allocations:

Total population size:\begin{aligned} N &= 600 + 300 \cr &\qquad + 100 \cr &= 1000 \end{aligned}
Calculate the quota for each stratum:\begin{aligned} \text{Petrol} &= \left(\dfrac{600}{1000}\right) \times 40 \cr &= 24 \cr \text{Diesel} &= \left(\dfrac{300}{1000}\right) \times 40 \cr &= 12 \cr \text{Hybrid} &= \left(\dfrac{100}{1000}\right) \times 40 \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}
Cars within each fuel type must then be selected using simple random sampling.

Final Answer: (a)(i) $28.5\text{ g/km}$ per litre increase, (ii) $78.2\text{ g/km}$, no practical validity, (b) $135.2\text{ g/km}$, (c) Line minimises vertical residuals, (d) Correlation does not imply causation, (e) $24$ petrol, $12$ diesel, $4$ hybrid

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $28.5\text{ g/km}$ total emissions, (ii) $78.2\text{ g/km}$, perfectly valid, (b) $135.2\text{ g/km}$, (c) Line minimises vertical residuals, (d) Correlation does not imply causation, (e) $24$ petrol, $12$ diesel, $4$ hybrid
pi_options.feedback: The gradient represents the rate of change per unit increase in $x$, not total emissions, and a 0-litre engine is physically meaningless.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $28.5\text{ g/km}$ per litre increase, (ii) $78.2\text{ g/km}$, no practical validity, (b) $135.2\text{ g/km}$, (c) Rearranging equations is algebraically invalid, (d) Correlation proves causation, (e) $24$ petrol, $12$ diesel, $4$ hybrid
pi_options.feedback: Algebraic rearrangement is mathematically valid, but statistically inappropriate because $y$ on $x$ minimises $y$-errors, and correlation never proves causation.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $28.5\text{ g/km}$ per litre increase, (ii) $78.2\text{ g/km}$, no practical validity, (b) $135.2\text{ g/km}$, (c) Line minimises vertical residuals, (d) Correlation does not imply causation, (e) $13$ petrol, $13$ diesel, $14$ hybrid
pi_options.feedback: Dividing the sample equally across strata ignores the population proportions of the three fuel types.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The One-Way Regression Rule
bradley_insight.content: A common exam question asks why you cannot rearrange $y = a + bx$ to find $x$. The answer is that the line of $y$ on $x$ is specifically fitted to minimise vertical residuals in $y$. Swapping roles requires calculating the line of $x$ on $y$.

topic: Data Presentation & Large Data Set Anomalies
question:
A student uses the Large Data Set to analyse daily weather records from a coastal location.

(a) In the Large Data Set, daily total rainfall values are recorded numerically, but on some days the entry is recorded as `'tr'`.
(i) State what the entry `'tr'` represents.
(ii) Explain how `'tr'` values should be treated when calculating the mean daily rainfall.

(b) The student generates a box plot using a spreadsheet package. The student notes that the software sets the whiskers to the minimum and maximum data values without identifying outliers.
(i) State the mathematical rule used to identify an outlier at the upper end of a data distribution.
(ii) Describe how outliers should be correctly presented on a standard box plot.

(c) To collect data on local attitudes toward weather warnings, the student interviews the first $30$ shoppers exiting a supermarket at $10\text{: }00\text{ am}$ on a Tuesday.
(i) Name this sampling method.
(ii) Give two distinct reasons why this sampling method is likely to produce a biased sample.
(iii) State one key difference between this method and quota sampling.
steps:
(a)(i) Meaning of 'tr':

`'tr'` stands for a trace amount of rainfall. It represents a non-zero rainfall measurement that is too small to record numerically (typically less than $0.05\text{ mm}$).

(a)(ii) Numerical Treatment of 'tr':

When calculating statistical summary measures such as the mean or standard deviation, `'tr'` values are treated numerically as $0$.

(b)(i) Upper Outlier Rule:

An upper outlier is any data value strictly greater than:\begin{aligned} Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR} \end{aligned}
where $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$.

(b)(ii) Presenting Outliers on a Box Plot:

Whiskers should extend only to the most extreme data points that are not outliers. Outliers should be plotted as individual separate markers (such as crosses or dots).

(c)(i) Sampling Method Name:

This is opportunity sampling (or convenience sampling).

(c)(ii) Sources of Bias:

1. Location bias: It samples only people who shop at that specific supermarket, excluding people who shop elsewhere or online.
2. Time bias: People shopping at $10\text{: }00\text{ am}$ on a weekday morning are likely to be retired or non-working, under-representing employed commuters and students.

(c)(iii) Difference from Quota Sampling:

In quota sampling, the researcher has predetermined category targets (such as specific numbers of people by age or gender) that must be filled. In opportunity sampling, the researcher simply interviews whoever is immediately available until the total sample size is reached.

Final Answer: (a)(i) Trace amount ($< 0.05\text{ mm}$), (ii) Treat as $0$ in calculations, (b)(i) $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, (ii) Whiskers to non-outliers and plot outliers separately, (c)(i) Opportunity sampling, (ii) Location and time biases, (iii) Quota sampling requires demographic targets

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) Thunderstorm reading, (ii) Omit from calculations, (b)(i) $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, (ii) Whiskers to non-outliers and plot outliers separately, (c)(i) Opportunity sampling, (ii) Location and time biases, (iii) Quota sampling requires demographic targets
pi_options.feedback: In the UK Large Data Set, 'tr' stands for trace rainfall, not thunderstorms, and must be treated as 0 rather than omitted.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) Trace amount ($< 0.05\text{ mm}$), (ii) Treat as $0$ in calculations, (b)(i) $Q_3 + 2.0 \times \text{IQR}$, (ii) Extend whiskers to outliers, (c)(i) Quota sampling, (ii) Location and time biases, (iii) Quota sampling requires demographic targets
pi_options.feedback: The standard IQR outlier multiplier is $1.5$, not $2.0$, and selecting whoever walks past without category quotas is opportunity sampling.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) Trace amount ($< 0.05\text{ mm}$), (ii) Treat as $0$ in calculations, (b)(i) $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, (ii) Whiskers to non-outliers and plot outliers separately, (c)(i) Systematic sampling, (ii) Location and time biases, (iii) Quota sampling requires demographic targets
pi_options.feedback: Systematic sampling requires an ordered sampling frame and an interval $k$; taking the first 30 available shoppers is opportunity sampling.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Handling 'tr' in the Large Data Set
bradley_insight.content: A perennial exam question on the Large Data Set tests how trace rainfall is handled. Never omit 'tr' values—that would bias your mean upwards. Always treat trace values as $0$ when calculating means or standard deviations.

subtopic: Regression Line of y on x
question:
A regional economic study investigates the relationship between the median annual household income, $x$ in thousands of pounds ($£1000\text{s}$), and the proportion of home ownership, $y\%$, across a sample of $30$ local authority districts.

The sample product moment correlation coefficient is calculated as $r = 0.624$.

(a) Stating your hypotheses clearly, test at the $1\%$ level of significance whether there is evidence of a positive correlation between median household income and home ownership rate.
(Critical value for $n = 30$ at the $1\%$ one-tailed level is $0.4226$.)

(b) The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is given by:
$$y = 0.82x + 31.4$$
The median incomes in the sample ranged from $£22\,000$ ($x = 22$) to $£58\,000$ ($x = 58$).
(i) Estimate the home ownership rate for a district with a median household income of $£45\,000$.
(ii) State, with a reason, whether your estimate in part (b)(i) involves interpolation or extrapolation, and comment on its reliability.

(c) The region comprises $240$ urban districts and $60$ rural districts. A researcher wishes to select a stratified sample of size $40$ based on district type. Calculate the number of urban and rural districts that should be sampled.
steps:
(a) Hypothesis Test for Correlation:

Let $\rho$ be the population product moment correlation coefficient.

Hypotheses:
$$H_0: \rho = 0$$
$$H_1: \rho > 0$$
For $n = 30$ at the $1\%$ one-tailed level, the critical value is $0.4226$.

Compare the test statistic:\begin{aligned} 0.624 > 0.4226 \end{aligned}
Because $r$ exceeds the critical value, reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $1\%$ level of a positive correlation between median household income and home ownership rate.

(b)(i) Estimating Home Ownership:

Substitute $x = 45$ into the regression line:\begin{aligned} y &= 0.82(45) \cr &\quad + 31.4 \cr &= 36.9 + 31.4 \cr &= 68.3\% \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Assessing Reliability:

The value $x = 45$ lies strictly within the range of sample data ($22 \le x \le 58$). This is interpolation, and because the linear correlation is strong and significant, the estimate is considered reliable.

(c) Stratified Sample Calculation:

Total population size:\begin{aligned} N &= 240 + 60 \cr &= 300 \end{aligned}
Calculate the sample size for each stratum:\begin{aligned} \text{Urban} &= \left(\dfrac{240}{300}\right) \times 40 \cr &= 32 \cr \text{Rural} &= \left(\dfrac{60}{300}\right) \times 40 \cr &= 8 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Reject $H_0$, significant evidence of positive correlation, (b)(i) $68.3\%$, (ii) Interpolation, reliable, (c) $32$ urban, $8$ rural

pi_options.ans: (a) Do not reject $H_0$, insufficient evidence of positive correlation, (b)(i) $68.3\%$, (ii) Interpolation, reliable, (c) $32$ urban, $8$ rural
pi_options.feedback: Because $r = 0.624$ is strictly greater than the critical value $0.4226$, $H_0$ must be rejected.

pi_options.ans: (a) Reject $H_0$, significant evidence of positive correlation, (b)(i) $68.3\%$, (ii) Extrapolation, unreliable, (c) $32$ urban, $8$ rural
pi_options.feedback: An income of $45$ lies inside the observed range of $22$ to $58$, making it an interpolation rather than an extrapolation.

pi_options.ans: (a) Reject $H_0$, significant evidence of positive correlation, (b)(i) $68.3\%$, (ii) Interpolation, reliable, (c) $20$ urban, $20$ rural
pi_options.feedback: Dividing the sample equally as $20$ and $20$ ignores the proportional representation of the urban ($80\%$) and rural ($20\%$) populations.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Greek Letters for Population Hypotheses
bradley_insight.content: Always state correlation hypotheses using the Greek letter $\rho$ (rho), representing the population correlation coefficient: $H_0: \rho = 0$. Using the sample statistic $r$ (e.g. $H_0: r = 0$) is a common error that will lose the hypothesis mark.

question:
The probability that Redstone HC wins a league hockey match is $\text{P}(W) = 0.45$, independently of all other matches.

(a) Calculate the probability that Redstone HC fails to win each of their next two league hockey matches.

The probability that Redstone HC loses a league hockey match is $\text{P}(L) = 0.35$.

(b) Explain why $\text{P}(W) + \text{P}(L) \neq 1$, and state the probability that a match ends in a draw.
steps:
(a) Probability of Failing to Win Two Consecutive Matches:

Find the probability of not winning a single match:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W') \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.45 \cr &\quad = 0.55 \end{aligned}
Since match outcomes are independent, multiply the probabilities:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W' \cap W') \cr &\quad = 0.55 \times 0.55 \cr &\quad = 0.3025 \end{aligned}

(b) Non-Exhaustive Outcomes and Draw Probability:

Winning and losing are not the only possible outcomes; a league match can also end in a draw ($D$).

Because winning, losing, and drawing are mutually exclusive and exhaustive:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W) + \text{P}(L) \cr &\quad + \text{P}(D) = 1 \end{aligned}
Calculate the probability of a draw:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(D) \cr &\quad = 1 - (0.45 + 0.35) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.80 \cr &\quad = 0.20 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $0.3025$, (b) Matches can end in a draw, $\text{P}(D) = 0.20$

pi_options.ans: (a) $0.2025$, (b) Matches can end in a draw, $\text{P}(D) = 0.20$
pi_options.feedback: Squaring $0.45$ rather than the complement $1 - 0.45 = 0.55$ gives the probability of winning both matches ($0.2025$).
Probabilities fail to sum to $1$ because the outcomes are not exhaustive, not because of a lack of independence.

pi_options.ans: (a) $0.3025$, (b) Matches can end in a draw, $\text{P}(D) = 0.10$
pi_options.feedback: An arithmetic error when adding $0.45 + 0.35 = 0.80$ incorrectly calculates $1 - 0.90 = 0.10$ for the draw probability.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Complementary vs Exhaustive Sets
bradley_insight.content: For probabilities to sum to $1$, the set of events must be both mutually exclusive and exhaustive. In sporting contexts with three outcomes (win, loss, draw), $W$ and $L$ alone are never exhaustive.

question:
A sports analyst models the outcomes of league football matches for a team. In any match, the probabilities of winning, drawing, and losing are modelled as:
$$\text{P}(W) = 0.50,\text { } \text{P}(D) = 0.20,$$ $$\text{P}(L) = 0.30$$
In the league competition, a team is awarded $3$ points for a win, $1$ point for a draw, and $0$ points for a loss. The outcomes of successive matches are assumed to be independent.

(a) State what is meant by the assumption that the outcomes of successive matches are independent.

(b) Find the probability that the team earns:
(i) exactly $4$ points from their next two matches;
(ii) at least $2$ points from their next two matches.
steps:
(a) Meaning of Independence:

Independence means that the outcome or result of any match has no effect on the probability of any outcome in any subsequent match.

(b)(i) Earning Exactly 4 Points:

A total of $4$ points from two matches requires one win ($3$ points) and one draw ($1$ point).

The possible sequences are $(W, D)$ or $(D, W)$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W, D) \cr &\quad = 0.50 \times 0.20 \cr &\quad = 0.10 \cr &\text{P}(D, W) \cr &\quad = 0.20 \times 0.50 \cr &\quad = 0.10 \end{aligned}
Summing these mutually exclusive sequences:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(\text{4 points}) \cr &\quad = 0.10 + 0.10 \cr &\quad = 0.20 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Earning at Least 2 Points:

The complement of earning at least $2$ points is earning fewer than $2$ points ($0$ or $1$ point):

Outcomes giving $0$ points:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(L, L) \cr &\quad = 0.30 \times 0.30 \cr &\quad = 0.09 \end{aligned}
Outcomes giving $1$ point:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(L, D) \cr &\quad = 0.30 \times 0.20 \cr &\quad = 0.06 \cr &\text{P}(D, L) \cr &\quad = 0.20 \times 0.30 \cr &\quad = 0.06 \end{aligned}
Total probability of the complement:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(< 2\text{ points}) \cr &\quad = 0.09 + 0.06 \cr &\qquad + 0.06 \cr &\quad = 0.21 \end{aligned}
Using the complement rule:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(\ge 2\text{ points}) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.21 \cr &\quad = 0.79 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Outcome of one match does not affect another, (b)(i) $0.20$, (ii) $0.79$
